18	# Looks Right, Works Right: A Project-Level Benchmark for Multi-Screen Mobile App Generation
19	
20	- Authors: Wu, Fan; Gao, Cuiyun; Huang, Yiming; Xiao, Yang; Chen, Yujia; Liao, Qing
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
22	- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Introduce MobileForge, a benchmark for project-level multi-screen mobile app generation from a folder of real app screenshots, with a five-axis evaluation (build, navigation, visual fidelity, code maintainability, efficiency), and use it to measure how far frontier multimodal LLMs are from producing a buildable, navigable, faithful and maintainable codebase [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- Opening question: "Can a multimodal LLM read a folder of mobile-app screenshots and generate the source code for that app?" [V] (p. 1). No formal hypotheses. The paper targets three gaps of existing benchmarks: single-page focus, no evaluation of interactive navigation, no project-wide maintainability measure [A] (p. 1).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction (VLM-drafted, human-reviewed annotations) plus a full-factorial evaluation of 6 models × 29 apps with a fixed agentic harness, single trial per cell; method studies of the visual judge (human alignment, cross-judge, protocol comparison); hand-labelled failure taxonomy [V] (pp. 3–8, 12–13).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: one tool-augmented agent receives all screenshots of an app plus the human-reviewed page-relationship description and must produce a React + TypeScript + Tailwind project in a pre-scaffolded directory; eight tools (write_file, read_file, str_replace, batch_str_replace, list_files, delete_file, run_command, task_done), soft six-phase plan, up to 50 iterations; on task_done an automated tsc + vite build feeds errors back [V] (p. 6). Prompting is fixed across models, with no screenshot-specific instructions or chain-of-thought, to attribute differences to the model [A] (pp. 6, 14).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: six closed models available April 2026 — Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash [V] (p. 6). No open-weight models and no non-agentic or prior-method baselines [I] (based on p. 6).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): 29 in-market consumer apps from official public distribution channels; screenshots captured manually from default-state or demo-mode screens without logging in [V] (pp. 3, 9).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 29 apps across 14 category buckets; 309 screens (mean 10.7, SD 3.8, range 5–21 per app); 701 navigation test specifications (mean 24.2, range 11–41 per app): 120 page-existence, 392 tab-navigation, 189 parent–child [V] (p. 3). Apps include Notion, Khan Academy, WhatsApp, Klook, Airbnb, Coinbase and others (Table 5) [V] (p. 12).
42	- Sampling / selection method: apps "prioritizing broad cultural recognition" [V] (p. 3) — a purposive, not random, selection. Annotation: a VLM drafts the page-relationship description and test specs; research-team annotators review every field; auto-drafts reach 96.8% recall / 94.3% precision (pages) and 74.1% / 83.9% (test cases); 64.7% of page and 76.5% of test drafts accepted unchanged [V] (p. 3, p. 15). The drafting VLM is not named — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement — not reported.
43	- Data availability (public? link?): https://github.com/anoa12159-hue/mobileforge_eval, research-only licence, with screenshots, annotations, harness, evaluator and all 174 run artifacts [A] (pp. 1, 9–10).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: single trial per (app, model) cell, 174 runs all completed [V] (p. 6). Build: clean Vite scaffold (React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind), `npx tsc --noEmit` and `vite build` must both pass with zero errors [V] (p. 4). Navigation tests run in headless Playwright (375×812 viewport) [V] (p. 5). Visual judge: Gemini 2.5 Pro, list-wise with k-shuffle = 3 and reference anchor over 29 apps × 701 scenarios [V] (pp. 6, 13). Sampling temperature and other decoding settings — not reported.
47	- Code availability: repository above; "one-command replay reproduces the comparison table verbatim" [A] (p. 10). Full system prompt only in the repository [V] (p. 14).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Build Success — both type-check and build pass; also route count, page-file count, route coverage [V] (p. 4).
51	- Navigation Correctness — NavPassRate: share of the 701 specs passed under state-isolated execution: each test starts by loading the source page route directly, performs the action, and passes if the URL matches the expected page or, for overlays, the page content hash "changes meaningfully" [V] (pp. 4–5). Rationale: chained walkthroughs cascade failures and blur attribution [A] (p. 5).
52	- Visual Fidelity — primary: per-model Borda score in [0, 1] from list-wise ranking by a VLM judge, with the original screenshot hidden among candidates as an anchor; rankings where the anchor is not first are discarded and re-run [V] (pp. 4–6). Secondary: point-wise 1–5 rubric (Layout 30%, Style 25%, Content 25%, Consistency 20%) kept as an absolute reference [V] (p. 6).
53	- Code Maintainability — total LoC; mean LoC/file (conciseness); ReuseRate (mean import count per shared component); DeadCompRate (share of declared components never imported); ColorConsistency (share of Tailwind colour tokens from a small recurring palette) [V] (p. 4). The authors use "maintainability" rather than "code quality" because correctness is covered by Build [A] (p. 4). These indicators are not validated against human maintainability judgements or established maintainability models — not reported.
54	- Efficiency — input/output tokens, LLM call count, wall-clock LLM time, dollar cost from list prices [V] (p. 4).
55	- Validation against human judgement (visual judge): 55 scenarios labelled with a blinded ranking interface — list-wise vs human strict Kendall τ = 0.716, top-1 accuracy 83.6%, top-2 overlap 80.4%, unrankable-set IoU 0.968; τ = 0.699 for page-existence and 0.731 for parent–child scenarios [V] (p. 13). The paper says "We labelled 55 scenarios" (p. 13), so the human reference labels appear to come from the authors themselves [I]; number of raters, expertise and inter-rater agreement — not reported. Cross-judge: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 139 scenarios from 5 apps gives inter-judge τ = 0.867 on the per-model ranking [V] (p. 13). Authors state no family self-preference is observed (Claude judge gives Claude candidates "slightly lower normalised Borda"; no numbers given) [A] (p. 13). Protocol smoke test (3 scenarios × 5 models): list-wise shuffle stability τ = 0.822, pair-wise position bias 23.3%, point-wise "ties-in-the-middle" [V] (pp. 12–13). Judge eligibility: Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5 ~100% anchor pass on a 33-scenario screening set; GPT-5.1 ~35% [V] (pp. 5, 13).
56	- Navigation evaluator validity: Table 11 reports false positives of the automatic evaluator among flagged cases (6% page existence, 1% parent–child, 10% tab navigation) [V] (p. 16).
57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilson 95% CIs for failure-mode proportions [V] (p. 8); ±1 SD error bars across apps in the cost plot [V] (p. 7). No significance tests for model differences; no run-to-run variance (single trial) [V] (pp. 6, 9).
58	
59	## 7. Key findings
60	1. Build success is 100% for all six models; authors attribute this to the harness's verify-repair loop, not the model [V] (pp. 6–7, 12).
61	2. NavPassRate: Opus 4.6 92%, GPT-5 89%, Haiku 4.5 85%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 82%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 62%, GPT-5 Mini 58% [V] (p. 7).
62	3. Visual fidelity has not saturated: Borda 0.906 (Opus) to 0.130 (GPT-5 Mini); point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5, so even the best model stays below 3/5; Opus leads in 26 of 29 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). The gap is concentrated in cross-page Consistency: models re-implement navigation chrome inline per page instead of sharing a component [A] (p. 6).
63	4. Maintainability is dissociated from visual fidelity: Opus writes 1,441 LoC (82 LoC/file) vs GPT-5 668 (33 LoC/file); GPT-5 has higher reuse (4.23 vs 3.83) and fewer dead components (7.8% vs 19.9%); ColorConsistency saturates at 0.74–0.85 [V] (pp. 6–7). Authors: "maintainability is uncorrelated with visual fidelity" [A] (p. 8) — no correlation coefficient is computed.
64	5. Cost: $0.15 (GPT-5 Mini) to $2.90 (Opus) per app; GPT-5 ($0.50, Borda 0.542, NavPass 89%) dominates Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on cost and quality [V] (p. 7). Cheaper models fabricate content (Lorem ipsum, stock imagery) [A] (p. 7).
65	6. Navigation failure taxonomy (n = 64 stratified hand-labelled failures from 3,486 executions): C1 blank starting page 7.8% [3.0, 18.3]; C2 route mapping error 10.9% [5.4, 20.9]; C3 target unreachable/occluded 32.8% [22.6, 45.0]; C4 click has no effect 48.4% [36.6, 60.4] [V] (p. 8). C4 (missing or mis-wired onClick) dominates for Opus and GPT-5 (75% of their labelled failures); C3 for GPT-5 Mini (67%); C1 for Gemini 2.5 Flash (42%) [V] (pp. 8, 15). Build checks do not catch silent event-handler bugs [A] (p. 8).
66	7. Per-app difficulty varies widely: point-wise visual 3.62 (Notion) to 2.01 (Apple News); NavPass 0.45 (Medium) to 1.00 (Khan Academy) [V] (pp. 7, 12).
67	
68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
69	- Single trial per cell; multi-trial replication left to future work [A] (p. 9).
70	- Visual scores come from Gemini 2.5 Pro, a competitor model class; mitigated by fixed judge, human calibration on 55 scenarios and a cross-judge check [A] (p. 9).
71	- Web-rendering proxy: output is React + Tailwind, not native iOS/Android; native APIs not exercised [A] (p. 9).
72	- Anchor-based judging depends on judges that follow the literal ranking instruction (GPT-5.1 fails) [A] (pp. 13–14).
73	- Per-model failure proportions (n = 8–12) are "descriptive signatures rather than precise point estimates" [A] (p. 8).
74	- Build success cannot discriminate models when a verify-repair loop is present [A] (p. 12).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] Input is not screenshots alone: the agent also receives a human-reviewed page-relationship description (tab structure, parent–child triggers) (pp. 3, 6), although related work frames the benchmark as using "only screenshots" without "any structural prior" (p. 2). Results therefore describe reconstruction with an annotated navigation map, not pure black-box observation.
78	- [I] Maintainability indicators are structural proxies (LoC, reuse, dead components, colour tokens) with no validation against developer judgement or standard metrics (complexity, duplication, smells, tests). LoC partly reflects how much content is reproduced, so "more LoC" is not clearly worse (p. 4, 7).
79	- [I] "Uncorrelated"/"orthogonal" is asserted from six model means (p. 8); no correlation is computed at app or run level.
80	- [I] Internal inconsistency in failure analysis: overall C4 = 48.4% (Table 4, p. 8), but the per-scenario-type projection (Table 11, p. 16) gives C4 of only 33% (parent–child) and 3% (tab navigation), which cannot average to 48.4% over the 581 interactive specs. The projection method or labels may differ; this needs clarification.
81	- [I] Human validation of the visual judge: 55 scenarios with unreported number of raters, rater expertise and inter-rater agreement (p. 13); the protocol comparison uses only 3 scenarios × 5 models (p. 12).
82	- [I] Human reference labels were produced by the authors themselves ("We labelled 55 scenarios", p. 13), not by independent raters, so the judge validation is not independent of the benchmark designers (blinding to candidate identity is stated, p. 13).
83	- [I] NavPass counts a pass when the content hash "changes meaningfully" for overlays (p. 5) — a lenient criterion; Table 11 shows 1–10% false positives in flagged cases (p. 16), but overall evaluator precision/recall on passes is not reported.
84	- [I] Well-known apps chosen for "broad cultural recognition" (p. 3) are likely represented in model training data; contamination is not discussed.
85	- [I] Single run per cell with stochastic agents; differences of a few NavPass points (e.g. Opus 92% vs GPT-5 89%) may be within run-to-run noise.
86	- [I] Navigation evaluated only as page transitions; in-page behaviour, state, data and back-end logic are not tested.
87	
88	## 10. Threats to validity
89	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): annotations drafted by an unnamed VLM, possibly from the same families evaluated; Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and evaluated model, and the only self-preference check is a qualitative comparison against one other judge (Claude Sonnet 4.5) on 139 scenarios from 5 apps (p. 13); human reference labels for the judge were produced by the authors themselves (p. 13); popular apps may be memorised [I].
90	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 29 apps, 5–21 screens each; web proxy instead of native; one harness design; closed models only [I].
91	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): NavPass measures routing, not full functional fidelity; Borda is relative (ordinal) and depends on the set of models compared; maintainability proxies unvalidated [I].
92	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single trial; no significance tests between models; Wilson CIs only for the failure sample (n = 64), per-model n = 8–12 [I].
93	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): strong — benchmark, harness, evaluator and run artifacts released, one-command replay (pp. 9–10); decoding settings and drafting VLM not reported; closed models may change [I].
94	
95	## 11. Future research directions
96	- Stated by authors [A]: multi-trial replication (p. 9); cross-platform/native extension (p. 9); stricter build gates (no `any`, strict null checks, lint) if compilation is to discriminate models (p. 12).
97	- Suggested by us [I]: test pure screenshot-only input (without the page-relationship description) and interaction recordings as input; add in-page behavioural tests and data/state checks; validate maintainability proxies against developer ratings and standard static-analysis metrics; report run-to-run variance.
98	
99	## 12. Relevance to our research
100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
101	- How it informs our work [I]: MobileForge is the closest existing design to our target study: it rebuilds whole multi-screen apps from screenshots of real, in-market apps with an agentic (vibe-coding-like) harness and scores functional navigation fidelity, visual fidelity and maintainability together. It shows these dimensions diverge (visual leader ≠ maintainability leader), giving direct support for joint evaluation. Its gaps — structural prior given as input, unvalidated maintainability proxies, single trials, no behaviour beyond navigation — are concrete design points for RQ5.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Propose DeclarUI, an automated approach that combines computer vision (CV), MLLMs and compiler-driven iterative refinement to generate multi-page declarative mobile UI code (React Native, Flutter, ArkUI) from UI design mockups or app screenshots, improving visual fidelity, navigation completeness and code quality [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- RQ1 Effectiveness: how does DeclarUI perform vs. baselines "when operating autonomously without human intervention"? [V] (p. 6)
33	- RQ2 Ablation: contribution of individual modules [V] (p. 6)
34	- RQ3 User study and manual repair: how do professional developers rate DeclarUI code vs. the baseline, and how much manual effort repairs compilation failures? [V] (p. 6)
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: technique proposal evaluated by a controlled comparison with two raw-MLLM baselines on a curated dataset, an ablation on a subset, a within-subject developer study, and a manual-repair timing study [V] (pp. 6–11).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: (1) Page Transition Graph (PTG) construction — Claude-3.5 infers nodes (pages) and edges (transitions with conditions/actions) from the design set as JSON; "designers or developers review the generated PTG, making necessary corrections or additions" [V] (pp. 3–4); (2) UI component extraction — Grounding DINO detection + Segment Anything segmentation + Claude-3.5 classification and functional description of each component [V] (p. 4); (3) prompt synthesis combining PTG, component analysis and the full screenshot [V] (p. 5); (4) iterative refinement — static-analysis check of implemented navigation vs. PTG (up to 3 iterations per page) and compile-error feedback (up to 3 iterations per project) [V] (pp. 5–6).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620 given unprocessed design images with "meticulously designed" prompts following prior image-to-code work, in React Native only [V] (p. 7). DeclarUI is run with GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 as base models; Flutter and ArkUI are run with DeclarUI (Claude-3.5) only, with no baseline [V] (pp. 8–9). No prior UI-to-code tool is used as a baseline [I] (based on p. 7).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): Figma community mockups (selected from 194 designs with >300 followers, ≥5 pages, mobile-specific) and Google Play apps (top 10 by downloads per category, excluding paid apps and complex registration; APKs installed on an emulator and screenshots captured manually) [V] (pp. 6–7).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: 50 apps (25 Figma, 25 Google Play), 5 logically connected pages each = 250 pages, 10 functional categories × 5 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). Ablation: 13 apps chosen by CLIP-score distribution across categories [V] (p. 9). User study: 12 apps stratified by CLIP score (3 > 0.85, 6 in 0.8–0.85, 3 < 0.8) [V] (p. 9). RAG experiment: 20 apps (100 pages) [V] (p. 11).
44	- Sampling / selection method: 3–5 per category per source, random selection of five when more available, "to control experimental costs while ensuring research quality and statistical significance" [A] (p. 7). Sample size limited "due to MLLMs' token cost constraints" [A] (p. 12).
45	- Data availability (public? link?): not reported in our PDF (no repository link found).
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: generated code inserted into an initial project in Android Studio (React Native, Flutter) or DevEco Studio (ArkUI) without manual intervention, built into an APK and run on the built-in emulator [V] (p. 8). Hardware: 2× RTX 3090, 64-core AMD EPYC, 512 GB RAM; custom Python scripts of 2,935 lines [V] (p. 8). UTG for evaluation obtained with DroidBot [V] (p. 7). Temperature, sampling settings and GPT-4o version: not reported. Image assets are excluded from evaluation [V] (p. 2).
49	- Code availability: not reported in our PDF.
50	
51	## 6. Evaluation metrics
52	- CLIP score — semantic visual similarity of generated vs original UI [V] (p. 7).
53	- SSIM — layout/structural similarity [V] (p. 7).
54	- PTG Coverage Rate PCR = |PTG edges ∩ UTG edges| / |PTG edges| × 100%, "manually calculated by human evaluators", comparing the predefined PTG with the DroidBot-explored UI Transition Graph of the built app — a navigation/functional-fidelity measure [V] (p. 7).
55	- Compilation Success Rate (CSR) — share of apps compiling after up to three automated refinement iterations [V] (p. 7).
56	- Average Compilation Iteration Count (ACIC) — compilation attempts per successfully compiled app (max 3) [V] (p. 7).
57	- Average Manual Correction Time (AMCT) — human repair time per compilation-failed app [V] (p. 7).
58	- Developer-rated code quality (user study, following Chen et al. [11]): Code Availability (proportion of generated code kept after modification to meet basic business requirements, tracked with git, mapped from 0.8 in 5% intervals to levels 1–5); Modification Time (5 points ≤5 min down to 1 point >20 min; 20-min cap per app); Readability and Maintainability (five-point Likert ratings) [V] (pp. 7, 9).
59	- Validation against human judgement: none for CLIP/SSIM; authors acknowledge they "may not fully capture human-perceived UI similarity" and state the user study "confirmed the validity of our evaluations" [A] (p. 12). No correlation between automatic metrics and human ratings is reported.
60	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Mann-Whitney U test for user-study ratings (p from 9.23E-08 to 2.57E-13) [V] (p. 10). No tests, CIs or run-to-run variance for CLIP/SSIM/PCR/CSR comparisons; no effect sizes — not reported.
61	
62	## 7. Key findings
63	1. React Native: DeclarUI (Claude-3.5) CLIP 0.88, SSIM 0.68, PCR 96.8%, CSR 98%; DeclarUI (GPT-4o) 0.87 / 0.58 / 88.6% / 88%; baselines GPT-4o 0.66 / 0.44 / 1.4% / 76% and Claude-3.5 0.65 / 0.41 / 43.3% / 74% [V] (p. 9).
64	2. Raw MLLMs largely fail to implement multi-page navigation (GPT-4o PCR 1.4%) [V] (p. 9). Baseline compilation failures came from non-existent packages/components, special-character handling and missing imports [A] (p. 8).
65	3. Generalisation: Flutter PCR 99.4%, CSR 92%; ArkUI PCR 95.9%, CSR 86% (DeclarUI Claude-3.5 only) [V] (p. 9). Knowledge-graph RAG for ArkUI on 20 apps: CSR 86% → 90%, AMCT 183 s → 43.5 s [V] (p. 11).
66	4. Ablation (13 apps): removing CV extraction drops SSIM 0.72 → 0.57; removing PTG + refinement drops PCR to 23.1% and CSR to 80% [V] (pp. 9–10).
67	5. User study (5 developers × 12 apps): DeclarUI vs Baseline (Claude-3.5) — availability 4.97 vs 4.15, modification time 4.03 vs 2.45, readability 4.62 vs 3.75, maintainability 4.55 vs 3.37, all p < 0.05 (Mann-Whitney U) [V] (p. 10). 73.3% of DeclarUI code modified within 10 min; 80% of baseline code needed >10 min [V] (p. 10).
68	6. Manual repair: AMCT 48 s (React Native, Claude-3.5), 43.2 s (GPT-4o), 62 s (Flutter), 183 s (ArkUI) [V] (p. 11).
69	7. Authors conclude generated code "meets industrial-grade standards" in availability, modification time, readability and maintainability [A] (pp. 1–2) — this rests on Likert ratings from five developers.
70	
71	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
72	- CLIP and SSIM may not capture human-perceived UI similarity; PCR does not reflect navigation fluidity or intuitiveness [A] (p. 12).
73	- Results depend on prompt design; user-study participant experience may bias results [A] (p. 12).
74	- Sample of 50 design sets may not represent all mobile UI types; limited by token cost [A] (p. 12).
75	- Uneven framework performance; ArkUI weaker, attributed to limited MLLM knowledge; RAG implementation limited by time [A] (p. 11).
76	- PTG construction could not be ablated alone because refinement depends on it [A] (p. 9).
77	
78	## 9. Limitations we identified
79	- [I] Human in the loop vs "autonomous" claim: the PTG is reviewed and corrected by designers/developers (p. 4), while RQ1 is framed as operating "without human intervention" (p. 6). How often and how much the PTG was corrected is not reported.
80	- [I] PCR is partly circular: DeclarUI receives the PTG as input and is checked against it during refinement, then scored against the same PTG (pp. 5–7); baselines never see the PTG. PCR also counts only edges, not correct behaviour on each screen, and is computed manually without reported agreement (p. 7).
81	- [I] Ablation numbers are internally implausible: on 13 apps, CSR values of 98.0% and 80.0% (p. 10) cannot arise (possible values are k/13, e.g. 76.9%, 84.6%, 92.3%). In the ablation table the "Full" row's CLIP/SSIM (0.90/0.72, p. 10) differ from the 50-app values (0.88/0.68, p. 9), while PCR/ACIC/CSR are identical to the 50-app run (96.8 / 0.22 / 98.0, pp. 9–10). This strongly suggests the visual metrics were recomputed on the 13 apps but PCR/ACIC/CSR were copied from the 50-app run (based on pp. 9–10); the ablation's PCR/CSR deltas are therefore not like-for-like comparisons.
82	- [I] User-study statistics treat 60 ratings per condition (5 developers × 12 apps) as independent; the tiny p-values (down to 2.57E-13, p. 10) overstate certainty (pseudo-replication). Blinding of participants to condition is not reported. Five participants is a small sample.
83	- [I] Code quality and maintainability are measured only subjectively (Likert) and by modification time; no static analysis, complexity, duplication or code-smell metrics.
84	- [I] Minor inconsistencies: Baseline Claude PCR 43.4% (p. 8) vs 43.3% (p. 9); ACIC defined as "number of compilation attempts" (max 3) yet reported as 0.22 (pp. 7, 9), implying it counts only repair iterations.
85	- [I] Single run per configuration; no variance across runs, though MLLM outputs are stochastic (sampling settings not reported).
86	- [I] Our PDF is arXiv v1 (18 Sep 2024); the FSE 2025 version may report different numbers.
87	
88	## 10. Threats to validity
89	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): human PTG correction; PCR scored against the method's own input; ablation subset chosen by CLIP score; possible training-data exposure of popular Google Play apps' UIs not discussed [I].
90	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 50 apps × 5 pages; only UI and navigation (no back-end, data, business logic); image assets ignored (p. 2) [I].
91	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): CLIP/SSIM unvalidated proxies for visual fidelity (p. 12); PCR measures presence of transitions, not their correctness of state; compilation success is a weak proxy for functional correctness; maintainability is self-reported [I].
92	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): Mann-Whitney on non-independent ratings; four tests without correction (not critical given p values); no CIs or effect sizes [I].
93	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): no code or data link in our PDF; model sampling settings missing; tools (Grounding DINO, SAM, DroidBot) named (pp. 4, 7) [I].
94	
95	## 11. Future research directions
96	- Stated by authors [A]: richer knowledge-graph RAG for less common frameworks such as ArkUI, dynamic KG updates, extension to other frameworks (p. 11); larger and more diverse UI samples (p. 12).
97	- Suggested by us [I]: report PTG correction effort; measure navigation and in-screen behaviour with automated GUI tests rather than manual edge counts; add objective maintainability metrics (static analysis, code smells) alongside developer ratings; use mixed-effects models for user-study ratings.
98	
99	## 12. Relevance to our research
100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
101	- How it informs our work [I]: DeclarUI is one of few studies that rebuilds multi-screen mobile apps from screenshots of existing Google Play apps — a direct form of reverse engineering from observable UI — and it measures navigation fidelity (PCR via DroidBot exploration), compilability and developer-rated readability/maintainability together. It shows that structuring the observable behaviour (page transition graph) and compiler feedback matter, but its maintainability evidence is subjective and its fidelity metrics have design weaknesses.
102	
103	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
104	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
105	|---|---|---|---|---|
106	| RQ1 | Pipeline: Grounding DINO + SAM component extraction, MLLM-built page transition graph, compiler/navigation feedback loop for declarative mobile UI code | p. 3–6 | V | moderate |
107	| RQ1 | PTG is reviewed and corrected by designers/developers (human in the loop) | p. 4 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ2 | Navigation fidelity via PTG Coverage Rate (manual comparison with DroidBot UTG): DeclarUI 96.8% vs Claude-3.5 43.3% vs GPT-4o 1.4% (React Native, 50 apps) | p. 7, 9 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | Compilation success 98% (DeclarUI Claude-3.5) vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs; CLIP 0.88 vs 0.65–0.66; SSIM 0.68 vs 0.41–0.44 | p. 9 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ2 | Without PTG + refinement, PCR falls to 23.1% | p. 10 | V | weak |
111	| RQ3 | Developer ratings (5 devs × 12 apps): readability 4.62 vs 3.75, maintainability 4.55 vs 3.37, Mann-Whitney p < 1e-11 | p. 10 | V | weak |
112	| RQ3 | Code quality/maintainability measured only by Likert ratings, code availability and modification time; no static metrics | p. 7, 9 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | CLIP/SSIM acknowledged not to capture human-perceived similarity; no correlation with human ratings reported | p. 12 | A | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | Ablation CSR values (98%, 80%) impossible for 13 apps; user-study test ignores rating dependence | p. 9–10 | I | moderate |
115	| RQ5 | No back-end/business logic, image assets ignored; sample 50 apps limited by token cost | p. 2, 12 | A | moderate |
116	
117	## 14. Key quotes
118	> "Finally, designers or developers review the generated PTG, making necessary corrections or additions" (p. 4)
119	> "This metric, manually calculated by human evaluators, assesses the alignment between the implemented app structure and the intended design." (p. 7)
120	> "CLIP Score and SSIM, used for UI similarity assessment, may not fully capture human-perceived UI similarity" (p. 12)
121	
122	## Analyst notes
123	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–13); reference list skimmed. Figure 7 heatmaps not inspected in detail (garbled in text; only summary statements used).
124	- Uncertainties: our PDF is arXiv v1 (Sep 2024), not the PACMSE/FSE 2025 published version; numbers may have changed. Ablation Table 2 numbers look inconsistent with a 13-app subset. Peer-reviewed (Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering, tier 1), but our copy is the preprint.
125

13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
17	
18	# WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch
19	
20	- Authors: Lu, Zimu; Yang, Yunqiao; Ren, Houxing; Hou, Haotian; Xiao, Han; Wang, Ke
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (published)
22	- DOI: 10.52202/085713-2419 · URL: https://doi.org/10.52202/085713-2419
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	- Version note: the PDF analysed is arXiv v2, "arXiv:2505.03733v2 [cs.CL] 11 Aug 2025" (p. 1), from arxiv.org/pdf/2505.03733. It is a pre-acceptance version, marked "Preprint. Under review." (p. 1), with the NeurIPS checklist appended (p. 37–43). Metadata records the NeurIPS 38 published version. Page refs refer to this arXiv PDF; the author line in the PDF (p. 1) lists Shi, Zhou, Zhan and Li and does not include "Hou, Haotian", who appears in `metadata.json` — the published author list may differ.
25	
26	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
27	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
28	
29	## 1. Research objective
30	[A] To measure how well LLM-based code agents can build complete, multi-file, interactive websites from scratch from natural-language instructions written for non-expert users, and to provide a training set that improves open models on this task (p. 1–3).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Stated contributions (p. 3):
34	- [A] A benchmark (WebGen-Bench) of website-generation instructions with test cases for functionality and appearance (p. 3).
35	- [A] An evaluation of three code-agent frameworks (Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider) with several LLMs (p. 3).
36	- [A] A training set (WebGen-Instruct, 6,667 instructions) and fine-tuned models (WebGen-LM 7B/14B/32B) (p. 3).
37	
38	## 3. Methodology
39	- Research design: benchmark construction; comparative evaluation of agent framework x LLM settings; validation of the automated judge against human testers; fine-tuning experiment with a training-size ablation (p. 4–10). [V]
40	- Approach / model / intervention: agents receive an instruction without technical details ("The agents should autonomously determine the optimal technical approach") and generate a website codebase from scratch (p. 5). [V]
41	- How functional correctness is tested: for each instruction GPT-4o drafted 5–10 atomic test cases (operation + expected result) covering every functional and appearance requirement; two CS PhD students independently reviewed and refined them and resolved discrepancies by discussion, giving 647 test cases (4–11 per instruction) (p. 5–6, p. 19). [V] Each test case is executed by the WebVoyager web-navigation agent driven by Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, which interacts with the site (at most 15 interactions), inspects screenshots and answers YES, PARTIAL or NO; if the limit is reached, a follow-up prompt forces a final decision (p. 6, p. 19–20). [V]
42	- How appearance is tested: GPT-4o grades screenshots 1–5 on rendering, content relevance, layout harmony and modernness (p. 6, p. 21). [V]
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: three frameworks on DeepSeek-V3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1; then Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, o3-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and the fine-tuned WebGen-LM models (p. 7–8). [V] No human-developer baseline. [V] (p. 7–8)
44	
45	## 4. Dataset and sample
46	- Data source(s): authors identified 20 web-application categories from freelance platforms (Upwork, Freelancer, Proginn); 40 CS PhD students brainstormed specific applications and requirements, producing 10,152 project descriptions; GPT-4o converted them into instructions with a one-shot prompt (p. 4–5, p. 15). [V]
47	- Sample size (N) and unit: test set 101 instructions; 647 test cases (p. 5–6). [V] Instruction categories: Content Presentation 28, User Interaction 49, Data Management 24 (p. 6, Table 2). [V] Test-case categories: Functional Testing 339, Data Display 186, Design Validation 122 (p. 23, Table 8). [V] These sum to 647 (339 + 186 + 122), matching the text (p. 1, p. 6). Table 8's printed "Total 667" is therefore an arithmetic or typographical error in that row (p. 23). [V]
48	- Sampling / selection method: "two to eight representative examples from each category" sampled for the test set; how representativeness was judged is not reported (p. 5). [V] Training set decontaminated by 5-gram Jaccard (> 0.6 removed) and sentence-embedding cosine similarity (> 0.55 removed), plus manual inspection of top-3 matches (p. 5, p. 14). [V]
49	- Data availability (public? link?): data, code and model weights released under MIT licence at github.com/mnluzimu/WebGen-Bench (p. 1, p. 14). [A] (link not checked by us)
50	
51	## 5. Experimental setup
52	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: Bolt.diy (browser-based WebContainer; model picks frameworks such as Vite/React/Remix), OpenHands with CodeActAgent, Aider with adapted prompts; OpenHands told to use TypeScript/HTML/CSS with `npm install` / `npm run dev`; Aider told to prefer Vite and Node.js (p. 7, p. 21–22). [V] Models smaller than Qwen2.5-Coder-32B were excluded because they often failed the output format (p. 7). [V] Sampling temperature, number of runs and time/step budgets for generation: not reported.
53	- Training: 2K WebGen-Instruct instructions run through Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-V3; trajectories kept only if the GPT-4o appearance score ≥ 3 (600 trajectories); Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct 7B/14B/32B fine-tuned for 2 epochs, LR 4e-5, batch 32 (p. 7). [V]
54	- Code availability: released (p. 1, p. 14). [A]
55	- Evaluator-reliability design: three human testers independently annotated the full test results of Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3; inconsistent cases went to a fourth tester for a final label; the agent's label was compared with this human label (alignment rate) (p. 8–9). [V] Appearance-score reliability: two extra model graders (o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet) and manual grading of the same three settings (p. 22–23). [V] Number of human appearance graders: not reported.
56	
57	## 6. Evaluation metrics
58	- Accuracy — (N_YES + 0.5 × N_PARTIAL) / N_total × 100% over all test cases; websites that fail to start count as failures (p. 7–8, Table 3). [V]
59	- Yes / Partial / No / Start-failed rates (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
60	- Appearance score — GPT-4o grade 1–5 (p. 6). [V]
61	- Alignment rate — share of test cases where UI-agent label equals the human label (p. 9). [V] Inter-human agreement among the three testers: "we assessed the consistency of their annotations" (p. 8), but no value is reported. No chance-corrected statistic.
62	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): none; NeurIPS checklist answers "No" for error bars "because it would be too computationally expensive" (p. 40). [V]
63	
64	## 7. Key findings
65	1. Best general-model setting is Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 at 27.8% accuracy (YES 24.7%), closely followed by Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet at 26.4% (p. 8, Table 3). [V]
66	2. Framework matters: with DeepSeek-V3, accuracy is 20.8% (Bolt.diy), 9.0% (OpenHands), 14.1% (Aider) (p. 8, Table 3). [V] Start-failure rates reach 38.6% (Bolt.diy + o3-mini) and 32.1% (Aider + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V]
67	3. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 filtered trajectories raises accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2% (WebGen-LM-32B), above DeepSeek-R1 (p. 8, Table 3); accuracy rises with training size: 25.1% (150), 31.9% (300), 38.2% (600) (p. 10, Table 6). [V]
68	4. Functional test cases are hardest: e.g. Bolt.diy + DeepSeek-R1 scores 21.1% on Functional Testing vs 44.3% on Design Validation; Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet 17.1% vs 52.0% (p. 9, Table 4). [V] The authors conclude that "superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities" (p. 8). [A]
69	5. UI-agent vs human labels: alignment rate 90.3% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet), 86.1% (DeepSeek-R1), 94.4% (DeepSeek-V3); aggregate accuracy differs by 0.4–2.3 points (agent 26.4/27.8/20.8 vs manual 26.0/30.1/21.3) (p. 9, Table 5). [V]
70	6. Best appearance score 3.0 (Bolt.diy + Claude-3.5-Sonnet) (p. 8). [V] GPT-4o, o3, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and human graders give the same ranking of three settings, with GPT-4o scoring highest (p. 23, Table 9). [V]
71	7. Human manual testing of all 647 cases is estimated at ~10.8 hours and $377.8 per setting (60 s per case), the stated reason for automation (p. 6). [V]
72	
73	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
74	- [A] Websites are generated only with TypeScript, JavaScript, CSS and HTML; Python, Java, Go and other tools were not integrated (p. 14).
75	- [A] Only supervised fine-tuning was used; RL or DPO not explored (p. 14).
76	- [A] Training data was not scaled beyond 600 trajectories because of API budget (p. 9).
77	- [A] No error bars, for cost reasons (p. 40).
78	
79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] The functional oracle is an LLM-driven UI agent with a 15-interaction cap (p. 19). Human validation covers only 3 of 16 settings, all Bolt.diy (p. 8–9); agreement may differ for OpenHands/Aider outputs or weaker models with many start failures. Alignment is reported as raw percent on a 3-class label without chance correction, and inter-human agreement is not reported (p. 8–9).
81	- [I] The alignment rate counts test cases; with 58–74% NO labels (p. 9, Table 5), a judge that says NO often gets high agreement by default. Per-class (YES vs NO) agreement is not given, so false-positive "YES" rates are unknown.
82	- [I] Test cases were drafted by GPT-4o from the same instruction the agent sees, and each checks one atomic requirement (p. 5, p. 19). They test whether a stated feature is visible and responds, not deeper behavioural correctness (data persistence, multi-step workflows, edge cases); "PARTIAL" earning half credit further softens the score (p. 7).
83	- [I] Minor typo: Table 8 prints "Total 667", but its main categories sum to 647 (339 + 186 + 122), matching the text (p. 1, p. 6, p. 23). This is a typo, not evidence of a different test set.
84	- [I] Single run per setting and no reported generation hyper-parameters (temperature, budgets) (p. 7–8, p. 40); differences of 1–2 points (e.g. 27.8 vs 26.4) are not separable from noise.
85	- [I] The models evaluated (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4o, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3/R1) are early-2025 models; absolute numbers are already dated relative to later benchmarks such as Vibe Code Bench (tran2026vibe) [I].
86	- [I] Fine-tuning trajectories were filtered by GPT-4o appearance score, not by functional tests (p. 7), yet gains are measured on functional accuracy; the training and test instructions share the same GPT-4o generation template and colour-requirement style (p. 15–18), so part of the gain may be format/style adaptation to the benchmark distribution despite n-gram/embedding decontamination.
87	- [I] No code-quality, security or maintainability measures are taken for the generated codebases.
88	- [I] Funding and conflicts: not reported in the main text.
89	
90	## 10. Threats to validity
91	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): framework prompts differ (OpenHands/Aider adapted prompts, p. 21–22), confounding framework comparisons with prompt design [I]. Decontamination of training vs test instructions is reported (p. 14) [V]. GPT-4o wrote instructions and test cases and is also an evaluated model (p. 5, p. 8) [V]; it scored low (12.8%), so no evident self-advantage [I].

97	## 11. Future research directions
98	- Stated by authors [A]: support more languages and tools for website generation; explore RL and DPO post-training (p. 14); add more training data or data augmentation (p. 9).
99	- Suggested by us [I]: report per-class judge agreement and inter-human agreement; validate the judge on all frameworks; extend test cases from atomic checks to multi-step workflows (as Vibe Code Bench does); add code-quality metrics; for reconstruction, generate test cases from an existing site's observed behaviour rather than from an instruction.

101	## 12. Relevance to our research
102	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (agent frameworks generating whole websites from NL instructions — Bolt.diy, OpenHands, Aider), RQ2 (functional fidelity via UI-agent test cases; headline accuracy), RQ4 (LLM-judge vs human alignment, test-case construction, no error bars), RQ5 (code quality not measured).

29	## 1. Research objective
30	[A] To provide an end-to-end software development (E2ESD) benchmark with fine-grained user requirements and executable behaviour-driven (BDD) tests, replacing the vague specifications and human or heuristic scoring of earlier benchmarks (SoftwareDev, SRDD), and to use it to assess LLM-based development frameworks (p. 1–2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	No formal RQs or hypotheses. The work addresses two stated problems of prior benchmarks: coarse-grained requirement specifications and unreliable evaluation protocols (p. 1). [A] Analyses ask how effective and efficient existing frameworks are, whether agentic frameworks improve on plain LLMs, and why they fail (p. 5–8). [V]
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: benchmark construction from existing open-source web apps with a human-in-the-loop multi-agent annotation pipeline (HITL-MAA); comparative evaluation of 6 framework types across 6 LLM backbones with 3 runs per task; human failure-mode analysis (p. 3–8). [V]
37	- Approach / model / intervention: generation side — Vanilla LLM, GPT-Engineer (single agent), Self-Collaboration, MapCoder, ChatDev, MetaGPT (multi-agent); OpenHands and SWE-Agent as reference systems (p. 5, p. 19–20). [V] Python-oriented frameworks were adapted to HTML/CSS/JS by changing system prompts (p. 19–20). [V]
38	- Benchmark construction (reverse-engineering direction): (1) GPT-4o agents insert `data-testid` attributes into the original source as stable DOM anchors (p. 3, p. 13); (2) a Code Analyzer Agent and Requirement Extractor Agent derive user-facing requirements from the source code, reviewed by human supervisors who check them against the running app (p. 4, p. 14); (3) a Test Case Generation Agent writes Gherkin Given–When–Then scenarios, reviewed and extended by five software-testing experts (p. 4); (4) a Test Automation Engineer Agent writes Python/Selenium step implementations, self-corrected by a dry-run verifier (max 3 iterations) and a test runner (max 6 iterations), with human fallback (p. 4–5, p. 13). [V] All tests pass on the original projects: "Validation on the generated dataset achieved a 100% pass rate across all executable tests" (p. 5). [V]
39	- How functional correctness is tested: the generated project is run in Chrome via Selenium and the Behave framework executes the Gherkin scenarios, giving deterministic pass/fail per test (p. 5, p. 29–30). [V] No LLM judge is used in scoring. [V] (p. 5) Generated apps must expose the same `data-testid` names, which are given in the prompt (p. 16–17). [V]
40	- Baselines or comparison conditions: Vanilla LLM is the reference baseline in all tables (p. 6). [V] HumanEval / HumanEval-ET runs of the same frameworks are used as a function-level contrast (p. 27). [V]
41	
42	## 4. Dataset and sample
43	- Data source(s): GitHub repositories found with keywords such as "mini project", "web application", "H5", over 500 stars (p. 12). [V]
44	- Sample size (N) and unit: 46 projects, 244 requirements (2–11 per project, mean 5.3), 703 BDD tests (mean 2.9 per requirement, 15.3 per project) (p. 3, Table 2). [V] Project types include calculators, CRUD/form apps and mini games; about one-quarter use local storage and another quarter external APIs (p. 18). [V]
45	- Sampling / selection method: five annotators screened candidates for executability, functionality and suitability (testable in about five minutes, no database or API-key setup); pilot Fleiss' kappa 0.47 → 0.83 after guideline refinement, 0.79 on an overlap subset; 46 of "over 158" shortlisted projects kept (p. 12–13). [V] The text describes the overlap subset as "10% of the full dataset (158 projects)" (p. 12) and then "over 158 initially shortlisted" (p. 13); the counts are inconsistent.
46	- Data availability (public? link?): code on GitHub and data on Hugging Face, CC-BY 4.0 data / MIT code (p. 9–10). [A] (links not checked by us)
47	
48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: backbones Claude-Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct ("Qwen-70B"), Qwen2.5-Max (p. 5, p. 19). [V] Six frameworks evaluated on all six backbones; OpenHands and SWE-Agent only on Claude-Haiku 4.5 and GPT-4o, OpenHands restricted to one execution without human interaction (p. 20, p. 22). [V] Effectiveness averaged over three runs; efficiency from a single run (p. 5, p. 20). [V] Decoding settings (temperature, seeds), maximum budgets per framework: not reported (ChatDev's 20-turn cap is mentioned, p. 24). The prompt contains the project summary, external resources and the refined requirements with `data-testid` names (p. 13, p. 16). [V]
50	- Code availability: released (p. 9). [A]
51	- Evaluator-reliability evidence:
52	  - Test-quality audit: 10 experts (5 original + 5 external) blind-reviewed a stratified random sample of 100 tests; Fleiss' kappa 0.81 (p. 14). [V]
53	  - Gold-checker protocol: four annotators validate each requirement/test, a senior "Gold Checker" consolidates only when Fleiss' kappa on equivalence, completeness and correctness exceeds 0.7 (p. 14). [V]
54	  - Human vs automatic: in the failure-analysis study "Cohen's Kappa" was 0.86 among human annotators and 0.74 between human and automatic evaluation (p. 22). [V] Which units were compared (requirements of the 360 projects?) and how many items were double-annotated are not reported.
55	  - Manual-only annotation pilot (no pipeline) gave Fleiss' kappa 0.23 on 14 test cases and ~80% executable tests (p. 15, p. 17, Table 5). [V]
56	
57	## 6. Evaluation metrics
58	- Req.Acc — fraction of requirements whose associated tests all pass (p. 5, p. 20). [V]
59	- Test.Acc — fraction of all tests passing (p. 5, p. 20). [V]
60	- Balanced score — 0.6 × Req.Acc + 0.4 × Test.Acc; weights chosen by the authors' "intuition" (p. 20). [V]/[A]
61	- Soft Req.Acc — allows partial requirement fulfilment (p. 5, p. 25); its exact definition is not given in the text we read. [V]
62	- Cost (USD from token prices), carbon footprint (estimated with A100 assumptions), duration (p. 5, p. 21). [V]
63	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): mean ± standard deviation over three runs (p. 6, p. 20). No significance tests or confidence intervals. [V]
64	
65	## 7. Key findings
66	1. Best effectiveness: GPT-Engineer + Claude-Haiku 4.5, Req.Acc 53.75 ± 0.43, Test.Acc 69.41 ± 1.07 (p. 6, Table 3). [V] Excluding MetaGPT, all Claude-Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o and Qwen-Max settings fall between 42.30 and 53.75 Req.Acc (p. 6). [V] The authors summarise: "achieving only 30%–50% Req. Acc." and no model exceeds 60% (p. 5). [A]
67	2. Soft Req.Acc exceeds Req.Acc by about 25–33 points in most settings (e.g. GPT-Engineer + Claude-Haiku 4.5: 0.5402 vs 0.7991), meaning partially working requirements are common (p. 25, Table 10). [V] Table 10's strict Req.Acc (0.5402) differs from the Table 3 value for the same setting (53.75, p. 6); see §9. The authors attribute this to failing edge cases and fine details (p. 6). [A]
68	3. Agentic frameworks do not reliably beat a plain prompted LLM: e.g. GPT-4o-mini Vanilla 44.82 Req.Acc vs ChatDev 33.16 and MapCoder 41.30; GPT-4o Vanilla 45.95 vs ChatDev 42.71 (p. 6, Table 3). [V] Cost (Table 3, p. 6) [V]: most multi-agent frameworks (MapCoder, ChatDev, MetaGPT) cost several times more than Vanilla, but the absolute costs are small:
69	   - GPT-4o ChatDev costs $0.1947 vs Vanilla $0.0160, about 12x.
70	   - Claude-Haiku 4.5 ChatDev costs $0.174 vs $0.015, about 11.6x.
71	   - On Qwen-7B, ChatDev costs $0.0075 vs $0.0003 (about 25x) and MetaGPT $0.0207 vs $0.0003 (about 69x). The Vanilla cost is rounded to 4 decimals, so these two ratios are imprecise.
72	
73	   Self-Collaboration, also a multi-agent framework (p. 5), costs about the same as Vanilla (Claude-Haiku 4.5 $0.014 vs $0.015; GPT-4o $0.0155 vs $0.0160) (p. 6). The paper itself states no cost ratio; the ratios above are our arithmetic on Table 3 [I]. All four multi-agent frameworks take longer than Vanilla on every backbone, e.g. GPT-4o: Vanilla 28 s; Self-Collaboration 37 s; MapCoder 93 s; ChatDev 114 s; MetaGPT 66 s (p. 6). [V]
74	4. MetaGPT almost completely fails (0.00–5.39 Req.Acc), attributed to inter-agent communication breakdowns: 44% of its failures are code inconsistency (missing files, syntax errors) (p. 6, p. 8). [V]/[A]
75	5. The same frameworks reach 71–91% Pass@1 on HumanEval (except MetaGPT), far above their E2EDev scores (p. 27, Table 12). [V]
76	6. OpenHands and SWE-Agent underperform the Vanilla baseline (Claude-Haiku 4.5: 43.45 and 44.73 vs 48.69 Req.Acc) (p. 23, Table 8). [V] The authors explain this by task mismatch with their original design (p. 22). [A]
77	7. Human failure analysis of 360 projects: four failure types (code inconsistency, requirement missing, requirement misaligned, detail mismatch); Vanilla LLM and ChatDev show the most missing requirements; Vanilla shows the fewest detail mismatches (p. 7–8, p. 23). [V]/[A]
78	8. The semi-automated pipeline needed human refinement for ~20% of requirements, ~50% of test cases and <20% of test scripts, at ~3.5 hours and ~$0.48 GPT-4o cost per project (p. 15–17). [V]

80	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
81	- [A] Small scale: 46 projects, because building repository-level executable tests is costly (p. 9, p. 30).
82	- [A] Web applications only; CI/CD workflows and deep backend inspection excluded for reproducibility (p. 9).
83	- [A] Pre-defined test scripts cannot be reused easily across methods because generated code structures vary (p. 30) — addressed by the `data-testid` anchors (p. 3).
84	- [A] OpenHands and SWE-Agent target different task settings, so direct comparison is "not conceptually equivalent" (p. 22).
85	
86	## 9. Limitations we identified
87	- [I] Tests are coupled to `data-testid` DOM anchors from the original app, and the prompt tells the model these IDs (p. 3, p. 16–17). A functionally correct app that names elements differently fails. Scores therefore mix behavioural correctness with instruction-following of naming conventions; how many failures are anchor mismatches is not reported.
88	- [I] The "human vs automatic" Cohen's kappa of 0.74 (p. 22) is the only direct validation of the automated oracle against human judgement, but its sample, unit and procedure are not described; Cohen's kappa is used although five annotators are involved, and 295 instances were "evenly distributed" (single-labelled) with only 5 shared calibration examples (p. 21). The kappa 0.86 among humans may therefore rest on very few items.
89	- [I] Inconsistent reporting: "four domain experts" in the main text (p. 7) vs "5 professional annotators" in the appendix (p. 21); "30 different models (6 backbones × 6 frameworks)" (p. 21) where 6 × 6 = 36; "10% of the full dataset (158 projects)" (p. 12) vs 158 shortlisted (p. 13). The strict Req.Acc values in Table 10 (p. 25) do not match Table 3 (p. 6). Most cells differ by under 1 point; some match exactly; a few differ more:
90	  - GPT-Engineer + Claude-Haiku 4.5: 0.5402 vs 53.75.
91	  - GPT-Engineer + GPT-4o: 0.5037 vs 50.83.
92	  - Qwen-7B ChatDev: 0.1803 vs 10.96, about 7 points.
93	
94	  This may be a single run vs the three-run mean, but the paper does not explain it.
95	- [I] Possible contamination: source projects are popular public GitHub repositories (> 500 stars) whose reference implementation is linked (p. 12, p. 17); models may have seen them. Not discussed.
96	- [I] Backbones are small or older models (Claude-Haiku 4.5, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5); no frontier coding models, so absolute ceilings are uncertain.
97	- [I] Projects are small, front-end-only apps that run from a local file without setup (p. 12, p. 17); backend, persistence beyond local storage, auth and deployment are out of scope.
98	- [I] Three runs give standard deviations, but some settings report ±0.00 (e.g. Qwen-70B and Qwen-7B Vanilla, p. 6), suggesting deterministic decoding for some backbones; decoding settings are not reported.
99	- [I] Requirements are detailed and implementation-near (e.g. exact class names and 150 ms timing, p. 16–17), unlike vague vibe-coding prompts; results speak to specification-following, not intent inference.
100	- [I] No code-quality or maintainability measures; "code inconsistency" in the failure analysis is a functional-defect category, not a quality metric (p. 23).
101	
102	## 10. Threats to validity
103	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): framework adaptations via system-prompt edits (p. 19–20) may disadvantage Python-oriented frameworks [I]; GPT-4o built the annotations and is also evaluated (p. 13, p. 16) [V]; anchor naming in prompts couples test outcome to instruction following [I].
104	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 46 small HTML/CSS/JS apps from GitHub (p. 3, p. 12) [V]; authors argue web is a "lower bound" for harder domains (p. 9) [A].
105	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): BDD tests validated on the original implementation (100% pass, p. 5) and audited by experts (κ = 0.81, p. 14) [V]; Req.Acc is strict (all tests must pass) and Balanced-score weights are arbitrary (p. 20) [V/I].
106	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): 3 runs with SD; no significance tests; many framework/backbone comparisons uncorrected (p. 6) [V/I].
107	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): code, data, prompts (Appendix G) and metric formulas released/printed (p. 9, p. 20–21, p. 31–37) [V]; decoding parameters not reported [V].
108	
109	## 11. Future research directions
110	- Stated by authors [A]: design "effective, reliable, and cost-efficient E2ESD solutions" (p. 9); expand E2EDev and maintain a public leaderboard (p. 9); reduce frameworks' reliance on strong backbones (p. 7); more robust stopping/exit strategies for multi-agent frameworks (p. 24).
111	- Suggested by us [I]: replace source-derived DOM anchors with anchor-free behavioural checks (e.g. browser-agent or accessibility-tree matching) so reconstructions are not penalised for naming; report human–oracle agreement per requirement with sample sizes; add code-quality metrics; test frontier coding agents.
112	
113	## 12. Relevance to our research
114	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (single- vs multi-agent generation frameworks for whole apps), RQ2 (functional fidelity measured by executable BDD tests derived from the original apps), RQ4 (test-oracle construction, kappa-based annotation quality, human–automatic agreement), RQ5 (no quality/maintainability; anchor-coupling issue).
115	- How it informs our work [I]: E2EDev is the closest benchmark design to reverse engineering in our set: it starts from existing applications, extracts requirements from their code and observed behaviour, writes behavioural tests that pass on the original, and asks models to rebuild the app from those requirements. This gives a concrete template for measuring functional fidelity of a rebuild against an original. Its weak point for our purpose is that tests depend on DOM IDs copied from the original source, which a true black-box reconstruction would not have. It also shows that agent orchestration adds cost without reliably adding fidelity.

30	## 1. Research objective
31	[A] To measure whether LLMs can carry out the complete "zero-to-one" process of building a working, deployable web application from a natural-language specification alone, judged by user-visible behaviour, and to check how reliable automated browser-agent evaluation is (p. 1, p. 3).

33	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
34	No formal RQs or hypotheses. Stated contributions (p. 1–2):
35	- [A] A benchmark and browser-based evaluation pipeline for end-to-end web-app development (p. 1).
36	- [A] A comparison of 16 frontier models including cost, latency and error analysis (p. 1–2).
37	- [A] An evaluator-alignment protocol with cross-model and human annotation (p. 2).

39	## 3. Methodology
40	- Research design: benchmark construction plus a comparative evaluation of 16 models in one fixed agent harness; secondary analyses (tool use, error taxonomy, reasoning-effort and vision ablations, variance decomposition, human-alignment study) (p. 4–9). [V]
41	- Approach / model / intervention: each model receives only a non-technical text specification and builds the app from scratch inside a modified OpenHands container with terminal, browser, Supabase/MailHog/Stripe services and MCP tools, up to 5 hours wall-clock per app (p. 3–4). [V] The system prompt mandates React + Vite, Tailwind, Supabase and Docker Compose (p. 4, p. 16). [V] The authors say a fixed stack was needed because otherwise apps "were too heterogeneous to evaluate consistently at scale" (p. 4). [A]
42	- How functional correctness is tested: pre-authored natural-language UI workflows (6–23 per task, each with substeps) are executed by an autonomous Browser Use agent (canonical evaluator model Claude Sonnet 4.5, vision on, headless 1920×1200, max 100 steps per workflow) against the deployed app; the agent produces pass/fail per substep ("LLM-as-judge substep judgments"); a workflow passes when ≥ 90% of substeps succeed; app accuracy = share of passing workflows (p. 4–5, p. 15). [V] If deployment fails, all workflows fail (p. 5). [V] The evaluator follows fixed workflow definitions rather than generating tests on the fly (p. 4). [V] Fresh browser session and unique account data per workflow to stop state leaking between tests (p. 5). [V]
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: 16 models from 9 providers compared with each other; no human-developer or commercial-tool baseline (p. 5). [V]

79	## 9. Limitations we identified
80	- [I] Functional fidelity is judged by an LLM browser agent, and the canonical evaluator (Claude Sonnet 4.5) belongs to the same family as several evaluated models (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku). Self-preference or style-familiarity bias is not tested: alignment was measured only on apps from Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (p. 8–9), and per-source-model agreement is not reported.
81	- [I] Agreement is raw percent agreement with no chance correction (p. 9). If most substeps pass or most fail, high percent agreement can coexist with low kappa. The very low GPT-5.2 agreement (31.8–48.0% with every other evaluator) is unexplained; agreement this far below the 84–94% of the other pairs may mean GPT-5.2 labels largely the opposite way, possibly through a systematic problem rather than ordinary judgment disagreement. One cue in the paper is consistent with this: GPT-5.2 evaluation costs $0.093 per workflow vs $1.48 for Sonnet 4.6 (p. 9), which would fit very short or terminated runs that are scored as fails when no structured output is returned (p. 5). The paper does not show this; it is speculation. Based on Table 10 (p. 9), costs (p. 9) and failure semantics (p. 5).
82	- [I] The alignment panel is small (18 apps from 6 tasks) relative to 50 test apps x 16 models; agreement is reported at substep level, while the leaderboard uses workflow-level pass with a 90% threshold. Workflow-level human–model agreement is not reported (p. 5, p. 9).
83	- [I] Main leaderboard numbers apparently come from a single generation per model per app (not stated; inferred from the SE definition, p. 5, and the separate variance panel, p. 8); ± SE reflects variation across apps, not across runs (p. 5, p. 8). Generation variance is large (SE up to 5 pp on the 6-app panel, p. 8), so adjacent ranks (e.g. GPT-5.2 vs Opus 4.6 Thinking, both 53.50) are not separable.
84	- [I] Specifications and workflows were drafted by GPT-5 (p. 3); a possible advantage for OpenAI models (top rank) is not examined.
85	- [I] The self-testing correlation is across only 16 models and is observational; the system prompt itself demands browser testing (p. 16, p. 19), so browser-call counts may reflect instruction following as much as testing skill. Identical r and partial r (both 0.72, p. 7) are reported without explanation.
86	- [I] Difficulty tiers are defined from the evaluated models' own pass rates (p. 6), so tier results are partly circular.
87	- [I] Subgroup cells are too small for comparison: in the test split Hard = 8 apps, Email + Stripe = 7, Email only = 4, Stripe only = 2 (Tables 5–6, p. 6); per-tier and per-integration averages rest on a handful of apps each.
88	- [I] The error taxonomy procedure (who labelled, how many failures) is not described (p. 8).
89	- [I] Authors are mostly from Vals AI, a company (p. 1); funding and conflicts are not reported. Not a model vendor, so no direct ranking conflict is visible.
90	- [I] The validation split is called "private" in the text (p. 1, p. 3) but "public" in Table 3 (p. 4); public availability of test tasks (and thus future contamination risk) is unclear.

92	## 10. Threats to validity
93	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): mandated tech stack and prompt reduce heterogeneity but make results harness- and prompt-specific (p. 4, p. 9) [V]. Evaluator same-family bias not tested [I]. Test-isolation measures reported (p. 5) [V].
94	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 100 expert-written greenfield specs, one stack, web only (p. 3, p. 9) [V]. Tasks start from a text spec, not from an existing app's UI or behaviour, so results transfer to reconstruction only indirectly [I].
95	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): browser workflows measure user-visible functional behaviour and are implementation-agnostic (p. 3–4) [V]; they do not capture code quality, security, visual fidelity or maintainability (p. 9) [V]. The 90% substep threshold is a design choice without sensitivity analysis [I] (p. 5).
96	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): SE across 50 apps reported; variance decomposition on 6 apps x 3 models (p. 5, p. 8) [V]; no significance tests; correlations with n = 16 [I].
97	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): unusually complete — prompts, hyper-parameters, evaluator settings, harness and trajectories released (p. 11, p. 15–23) [V]; evaluator uses provider-default sampling parameters, with no override set in the evaluator code (Table 16, p. 15) [V]; seeds are not reported.

99	## 11. Future research directions
100	- Stated by authors [A]: extending "zero-to-one" evaluation to CLI, desktop and mobile apps; testing other harnesses and stacks; measuring readability, visual design and security (implied by the limitations list, p. 9). Treat evaluator choice as "a first-class reporting concern" (p. 9).
101	- Suggested by us [I]: reuse the browser-workflow oracle for reconstruction tasks — run the same workflows on the original app and the rebuilt app to score behavioural fidelity; add static-analysis and maintainability metrics on the generated repositories (which the authors release); report chance-corrected agreement and workflow-level human–judge agreement.

103	## 12. Relevance to our research
104	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (agentic vibe-coding generation of full web apps from text specs), RQ2 (functional fidelity via browser workflows; headline accuracy), RQ3 (explicitly not measured — useful as negative evidence), RQ4 (LLM-judge reliability, human alignment, variance decomposition), RQ5 (authors' own call for code-quality measurement).
105	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest benchmark to a vibe-coding rebuild: a non-technical spec in, a deployed multi-page app out, judged only through the browser like a user. Its evaluation design (pre-authored natural-language workflows run by a browser agent, with a human-alignment check) is a ready template for measuring functional fidelity of a reconstructed app against the original. It also shows that the judge itself is a major source of measurement error (36% vs 86% human agreement depending on judge model), and that code quality and maintainability remain unmeasured.

28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Test whether current LLMs can generate *application-level* repositories (runnable, multi-file, with dependencies, executable end to end) that satisfy both functional correctness and non-functional quality attributes. The authors argue that function-, contest-, repo-completion- and feature-level benchmarks do not test this (p. 1).
30	- [A] Introduce RAL-Bench (Real-World Application-Level Code Generation Bench): a benchmark and evaluation framework that derives a natural-language requirement from a real reference project and tests generated repositories with reference-validated black-box system tests (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [V] RQ1: how well current LLMs perform at application-level generation; RQ2: where they fail; RQ3: what it costs; RQ4: whether mainstream generation strategies help (p. 5).
34	- No formal hypotheses stated.

36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Benchmark construction, then a controlled, single-turn, zero-shot comparison of 16 LLMs, plus a manual failure taxonomy, a cost analysis, a single-model strategy ablation, and prompt-sensitivity and metric-robustness checks (p. 4; p. 5; p. 9).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each LLM receives (a) a short NL requirement drafted from the reference project's README, public API, usage examples and source code, then manually edited to remove implementation details, file-layout hints and project-specific names, and (b) the reference repository's expected module/package surface (an "interface specification"). It outputs the whole repository in one pass (p. 2; p. 4; p. 5). [V] For GPT-5.2 on Stegano, adding the interface specification raised the functional score from 0.1667 to 0.6667, attributed to fewer entry-point/module-path mismatches (p. 4).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 11 "standard" and 5 "thinking" LLMs are compared with each other. There is no non-LLM or human baseline; the reference repository is used only as a normalisation anchor for non-functional scores (p. 4; p. 5). [V] RQ4 compares the GPT-5.2 baseline with three one-shot strategies: S1 feedback-driven self-repair, S2 automated environment repair, S3 planning-driven generation (p. 8).
40	- [I] Relation to our topic: the "reference" is a real application, and generated code is judged on tests that pass on that reference. This is close to rebuilding an existing app from its specification. However, the model never sees or runs the reference. It gets a distilled text requirement plus the API surface, so this is spec-to-app generation, not black-box behavioural reverse engineering.

Sizes range from 1 to 242 files and 0.3k to 109.5k LoC (p. 2).

45	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Three criteria: clearly documented functionality, stable public interfaces suitable for end-to-end tests, and active real-world use. Average popularity is above 1,000 stars, and repositories already used in public code-generation benchmarks are excluded (p. 2). How the 38 were picked from the candidate pool: not reported.

48	## 5. Experimental setup
49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Zero-shot, each model's default prompt template, the whole repository generated in one pass within context limits, three repeats averaged (p. 5). [A] The abstract says "greedy decoding" (p. 1). The setup section does not restate temperature or decoding parameters (not reported in Section 3.1). [V] Tests are pytest suites run against the generated repository; the functional score is the pass ratio (p. 3; p. 4). [V] Non-functional pipeline (p. 3; p. 4):
50	  - maintainability: lower-bound Maintainability Index (MI) from static analysis;
51	  - security: number of high-risk static-analysis findings;
52	  - robustness: pass rate on an invalid/boundary-input suite;
53	  - efficiency: runtime of an efficiency suite;
54	  - resource: average RSS memory and CPU during a resource suite.

56	  Each is normalised against the reference repository and capped at 1. The static-analysis tools are not named in the text; Fig. 3 shows only "mi_min" and "high_risk_count" (p. 4). [V] Aggregate NF = 0.36 M + 0.24 S + 0.16 Rb + 0.12 E + 0.12 Ru. The weights come from AHP (analytic hierarchy process, a method that turns pairwise importance judgements into weights) applied to an ordering taken from Botchway et al.; consistency ratio 0.030 (p. 4).
57	- [V] Rerun stability: the full pipeline was rerun 5 times for GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and Claude-4.5-Sonnet (p. 6; p. 7).

61	## 6. Evaluation metrics
62	- Functional score: pass rate of reference-validated black-box functional tests. Chosen because it "directly measures whether the generated application behavior matches the reference implementation's intended functionality" (p. 4).
63	- Maintainability M = (g/b)/(1+g/b), where g and b are the MI lower bounds of the generated and reference code. Called a "low-cost and reproducible signal of structural complexity"; the authors note that it misses naming quality and architectural clarity (p. 3).
64	- Security S = min(1, (b+1)/(g+1)) over high-risk static findings, described as a "conservative risk signal" (p. 3).
65	- Robustness Rb is the pass ratio of the robustness suite. Efficiency E = min(1, Tref/Tgen), set to 0 if the suite fails. Resource Ru is the mean of the capped memory and CPU ratios, set to 0 if the suite fails (p. 3; p. 4).
66	- Non-functional score NF: AHP-weighted sum of the five dimensions (p. 4).
67	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] No significance tests, confidence intervals or effect sizes. The paper reports only means over 3 runs and Std/CV over 5 reruns (p. 5; p. 7). [V] Metric robustness is checked with Spearman rank correlation of model rankings under alternative aggregations (p. 10).
68	
69	## 7. Key findings
70	1. [V] Functional correctness is low. The average functional score is 33.98% for standard and 30.23% for thinking LLMs, and no model exceeds 45%. Best: Gemini-3-Pro-Preview 43.86% and Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking 43.44%; lowest: DeepSeek-R1 16.23% (p. 5; p. 6).
71	2. [V] Non-functional averages are higher: 52.25% for standard and 49.57% for thinking LLMs. For standard LLMs, average maintainability is 33.45% and security 87.40% (p. 5; p. 6).
72	3. [V] NF separates models that functional scores do not: Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4o have almost equal functional scores (27.63% vs 27.48%) but NF of 35.15% vs 57.59% (p. 5).
73	4. [V] Thinking models are not consistently better and on average score slightly below standard LLMs (p. 6).
74	5. [V] Failure taxonomy: requirement–implementation mismatches plus non-functional quality failures make up 82.8% of failures; executability/dependency failures make up 17.2% (p. 7).
75	6. [V] Cost per run ranges from $0.15 (DeepSeek-V3.2) to $16.63 (Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking), averaging $4.10 for standard and $11.00 for thinking models. Higher cost does not reliably buy a higher functional score (p. 8).
76	7. [V] On GPT-5.2, none of the three one-shot strategies beat the baseline (41.80% functional, 57.10% NF). S1 scored 37.70/46.10, S2 40.20/49.90 and S3 41.20/49.60; all three lowered NF (p. 8; p. 9).
77	8. [V] Prompt variants moved GPT-5.2's mean functional score from 0.4181 (baseline) to 0.4972 (clarified) and 0.4919 (paraphrased). The authors call the differences small (p. 9).
78	9. [V] Functional scores had Std = 0 and CV = 0 across 5 reruns for all three models and all 38 projects; the median NF CV was 0.0007 (p. 6; p. 7).
79	10. [V] The NF model ranking is stable under equal weights, uncapped normalisation and leave-one-out variants (Spearman 0.90–0.99), but not under a rank-based aggregate (0.6441) (p. 10).
80	11. [V] Defect-injection sanity check: the functional suites detected all 76 injected defects (2 per task); the robustness suites detected 0.375 of them (p. 5).
