82	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
83	- [A] The repositories are public, so pretraining exposure cannot be ruled out. Results are interpreted as reflecting "realistic public-repository exposure conditions" (p. 2).
84	- [A] Validating tests on the reference repository supports oracle validity but does not guarantee full behavioural coverage (p. 3).
85	- [A] MI does not capture naming quality or architectural clarity. Static security analysis can give false positives and false negatives. Runtime measures depend on the environment. The metrics are operational proxies, not an expert audit (p. 3; p. 4).
86	- [A] The single-turn zero-shot protocol does not represent iterative or agentic workflows; a multi-turn/agentic study is future work (p. 4; p. 5).
87	- [A] The strategy study (RQ4) uses a single model and is not a ranking of strategy families (p. 8).
88	- [A] The AHP weights are not claimed to be universal across domains (p. 4).
89	
90	## 9. Limitations we identified
91	- [I] The oracles are small. About 11 functional tests per task (p. 5) is a thin behavioural specification for projects of up to 109.5k LoC (p. 2). The 100% defect-detection rate rests on only 2 injected defects per task, and their type and injection method are not described (p. 5). It does not show that the suites would catch subtle divergences.
92	- [I] Contamination is likely, not just possible. The example requirement in Fig. 2/3 asks for code that "is API-compatible with the core parts of the Stegano project" (p. 3; p. 4), naming the original even though project-specific names were supposedly removed (p. 2). In the Celery failure case, the generated code references `celery.utils.threads`, "consistent with upstream Celery internals" (p. 9), which suggests recall of the original code. Together with the supplied module/package surface (p. 4), the task partly tests memory of well-known Python libraries.
93	- [I] The non-functional metrics can reward incomplete code. Maintainability and security are static and are computed whatever the functional result. A small or partial repository naturally has fewer high-risk findings and simpler structure. GPT-3.5-Turbo's 97.37% security score next to its 29.76% functional score (p. 6) fits this reading. NF therefore mixes "quality" with "less code". Only efficiency and resource are set to 0 when their suites fail (p. 3).
94	- [I] The maintainability score M = (g/b)/(1+g/b) equals 0.5 when the generated MI equals the reference MI and approaches 1 only when the generated MI is much higher (p. 3). M is therefore on a different scale from the other four dimensions, yet it carries the largest weight (0.36) (p. 4). An average M of about 33% (p. 6) suggests that the typical generated repository has a lower MI lower bound than the reference, but the paper reports no raw MI values to confirm this.
95	- [I] Zero variance in functional scores across 5 full reruns (p. 7) is surprising for API-served LLMs generating whole repositories, even with greedy decoding. Either the reruns re-evaluated cached generations, or the models were unusually deterministic. The paper does not say which, so the stability claim may describe the test harness rather than generation.
96	- [I] The 446 repositories in the failure analysis (p. 7) do not match 16 models x 38 tasks (608 per run), and how they were selected is not reported. Who assigned the failure categories, and whether agreement was measured, is also not reported.
97	- [I] The prompt-sensitivity result (0.4181 to 0.4972, about +8 points or +19% relative) (p. 9) is not "small" compared with the model spread: functional scores range 16.23–43.86% (27.6 pp) over all 16 models, and 24.37–43.86% (19.5 pp) without DeepSeek-R1 (Tables 4–5, p. 6). The +7.9 pp prompt effect is about 30–40% of that spread. Requirement wording may matter as much as model choice.
98	- [I] All 38 projects are Python (p. 2). Some have user-facing interfaces (e.g. mitmproxy, Mailpile, glances, folium in Table 1, p. 2), but they are evaluated only through black-box pytest suites built from documented behaviours and public APIs (p. 2; pytest invocations, p. 3); UI behaviour is never exercised, so the findings transfer only partly to UI-level reconstruction.
99	- [I] "Maintainability" is reduced to one complexity index. Code smells, duplication, modularity and human judgement of the generated code are not measured.
100	
101	## 10. Threats to validity
102	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Requirements were drafted with access to the source code (p. 2), tests were built from the reference's documented behaviour (p. 2), and the interface specification reveals the module layout (p. 4). Contamination with the original public code is plausible (see section 9). Who drafted and reviewed the requirements and tests, and with what tool support, is not reported.
103	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 38 Python projects, tested only through their public APIs (p. 2), not their UIs. Generation is single-turn and zero-shot without agents (p. 4; p. 5), unlike vibe-coding practice where developers iterate with agents.
104	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] The functional score is a pass rate on about 11 tests (p. 5), maintainability is the MI lower bound only (p. 3), and security is a count of high-risk static findings. These are weak proxies for "functional fidelity" and "maintainability" as our project defines them, which the authors acknowledge (p. 4).
105	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No tests or intervals. Model differences of a few points (e.g. 27.63 vs 27.48) are discussed only descriptively (p. 5). Results are means of three runs (p. 5).
106	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [A] Code and data are public (p. 11), and commits are pinned (p. 2). [I] Decoding parameters appear only in the abstract, and the static-analysis tools are not named in the text.
107	
108	## 11. Future research directions
109	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 10; p. 11):
110	  - requirement analysis that turns short NL requests into explicit specifications with behaviours and edge cases;
111	  - cross-module repair using application-level feedback;
112	  - quality-aware generation that treats robustness, efficiency, resources, maintainability and security as explicit constraints;
113	  - extending RAL-Bench to more projects and to multi-turn/agentic settings (p. 5).
114	- Suggested by us [I]:
115	  1. Run the same reference-validated test design in an agentic, iterative (vibe-coding-like) setting.
116	  2. Report raw MI and add richer maintainability measures that do not depend on code size (smells, duplication, modularity, change-effort experiments).
117	  3. Test with obfuscated project names and without the interface specification to estimate contamination.
118	  4. Extend the design to applications with UIs.
119	
120	## 12. Relevance to our research
121	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 (secondary RQ1).
122	- How it informs our work [I]: This is one of the few studies that measures both functional correctness and maintainability of the same generated applications against the original project, using the original as test oracle and as normalisation anchor. That is the joint fidelity-plus-quality design that RQ5 asks about. Its weaknesses (thin oracles, MI-only maintainability, single-turn generation, contamination) are exactly what a new study should improve. Its finding that one-shot repair and planning lowered non-functional quality (p. 8) is a direct warning for vibe-coding workflows that iterate on failures.

18	# Looks Right, Works Right: A Project-Level Benchmark for Multi-Screen Mobile App Generation
19	
20	- Authors: Wu, Fan; Gao, Cuiyun; Huang, Yiming; Xiao, Yang; Chen, Yujia; Liao, Qing
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
22	- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.2650
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Introduce MobileForge, a benchmark for project-level multi-screen mobile app generation from a folder of real app screenshots, with a five-axis evaluation (build, navigation, visual fidelity, code maintainability, efficiency), and use it to measure how far frontier multimodal LLMs are from producing a buildable, navigable, faithful and maintainable codebase [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- Opening question: "Can a multimodal LLM read a folder of mobile-app screenshots and generate the source code for that app?" [V] (p. 1). No formal hypotheses. The paper targets three gaps of existing benchmarks: single-page focus, no evaluation of interactive navigation, no project-wide maintainability measure [A] (p. 1).
33	
34	## 3. Methodology
35	- Research design: benchmark construction (VLM-drafted, human-reviewed annotations) plus a full-factorial evaluation of 6 models × 29 apps with a fixed agentic harness, single trial per cell; method studies of the visual judge (human alignment, cross-judge, protocol comparison); hand-labelled failure taxonomy [V] (pp. 3–8, 12–13).
36	- Approach / model / intervention: one tool-augmented agent receives all screenshots of an app plus the human-reviewed page-relationship description and must produce a React + TypeScript + Tailwind project in a pre-scaffolded directory; eight tools (write_file, read_file, str_replace, batch_str_replace, list_files, delete_file, run_command, task_done), soft six-phase plan, up to 50 iterations; on task_done an automated tsc + vite build feeds errors back [V] (p. 6). Prompting is fixed across models, with no screenshot-specific instructions or chain-of-thought, to attribute differences to the model [A] (pp. 6, 14).
37	- Baselines or comparison conditions: six closed models available April 2026 — Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash [V] (p. 6). No open-weight models and no non-agentic or prior-method baselines [I] (based on p. 6).
38	
39	## 4. Dataset and sample
40	- Data source(s): 29 in-market consumer apps from official public distribution channels; screenshots captured manually from default-state or demo-mode screens without logging in [V] (pp. 3, 9).
41	- Sample size (N) and unit: 29 apps across 14 category buckets; 309 screens (mean 10.7, SD 3.8, range 5–21 per app); 701 navigation test specifications (mean 24.2, range 11–41 per app): 120 page-existence, 392 tab-navigation, 189 parent–child [V] (p. 3). Apps include Notion, Khan Academy, WhatsApp, Klook, Airbnb, Coinbase and others (Table 5) [V] (p. 12).
42	- Sampling / selection method: apps "prioritizing broad cultural recognition" [V] (p. 3) — a purposive, not random, selection. Annotation: a VLM drafts the page-relationship description and test specs; research-team annotators review every field; auto-drafts reach 96.8% recall / 94.3% precision (pages) and 74.1% / 83.9% (test cases); 64.7% of page and 76.5% of test drafts accepted unchanged [V] (p. 3, p. 15). The drafting VLM is not named — not reported. Inter-annotator agreement — not reported.
43	- Data availability (public? link?): https://github.com/anoa12159-hue/mobileforge_eval, research-only licence, with screenshots, annotations, harness, evaluator and all 174 run artifacts [A] (pp. 1, 9–10).
44	
45	## 5. Experimental setup
46	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: single trial per (app, model) cell, 174 runs all completed [V] (p. 6). Build: clean Vite scaffold (React 19 + TypeScript + Tailwind), `npx tsc --noEmit` and `vite build` must both pass with zero errors [V] (p. 4). Navigation tests run in headless Playwright (375×812 viewport) [V] (p. 5). Visual judge: Gemini 2.5 Pro, list-wise with k-shuffle = 3 and reference anchor over 29 apps × 701 scenarios [V] (pp. 6, 13). Sampling temperature and other decoding settings — not reported.
47	- Code availability: repository above; "one-command replay reproduces the comparison table verbatim" [A] (p. 10). Full system prompt only in the repository [V] (p. 14).
48	
49	## 6. Evaluation metrics
50	- Build Success — both type-check and build pass; also route count, page-file count, route coverage [V] (p. 4).
51	- Navigation Correctness — NavPassRate: share of the 701 specs passed under state-isolated execution: each test starts by loading the source page route directly, performs the action, and passes if the URL matches the expected page or, for overlays, the page content hash "changes meaningfully" [V] (pp. 4–5). Rationale: chained walkthroughs cascade failures and blur attribution [A] (p. 5).
52	- Visual Fidelity — primary: per-model Borda score in [0, 1] from list-wise ranking by a VLM judge, with the original screenshot hidden among candidates as an anchor; rankings where the anchor is not first are discarded and re-run [V] (pp. 4–6). Secondary: point-wise 1–5 rubric (Layout 30%, Style 25%, Content 25%, Consistency 20%) kept as an absolute reference [V] (p. 6).
53	- Code Maintainability — total LoC; mean LoC/file (conciseness); ReuseRate (mean import count per shared component); DeadCompRate (share of declared components never imported); ColorConsistency (share of Tailwind colour tokens from a small recurring palette) [V] (p. 4). The authors use "maintainability" rather than "code quality" because correctness is covered by Build [A] (p. 4). These indicators are not validated against human maintainability judgements or established maintainability models — not reported.
54	- Efficiency — input/output tokens, LLM call count, wall-clock LLM time, dollar cost from list prices [V] (p. 4).
55	- Validation against human judgement (visual judge): 55 scenarios labelled with a blinded ranking interface — list-wise vs human strict Kendall τ = 0.716, top-1 accuracy 83.6%, top-2 overlap 80.4%, unrankable-set IoU 0.968; τ = 0.699 for page-existence and 0.731 for parent–child scenarios [V] (p. 13). The paper says "We labelled 55 scenarios" (p. 13), so the human reference labels appear to come from the authors themselves [I]; number of raters, expertise and inter-rater agreement — not reported. Cross-judge: Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 139 scenarios from 5 apps gives inter-judge τ = 0.867 on the per-model ranking [V] (p. 13). Authors state no family self-preference is observed (Claude judge gives Claude candidates "slightly lower normalised Borda"; no numbers given) [A] (p. 13). Protocol smoke test (3 scenarios × 5 models): list-wise shuffle stability τ = 0.822, pair-wise position bias 23.3%, point-wise "ties-in-the-middle" [V] (pp. 12–13). Judge eligibility: Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5 ~100% anchor pass on a 33-scenario screening set; GPT-5.1 ~35% [V] (pp. 5, 13).
56	- Navigation evaluator validity: Table 11 reports false positives of the automatic evaluator among flagged cases (6% page existence, 1% parent–child, 10% tab navigation) [V] (p. 16).
57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilson 95% CIs for failure-mode proportions [V] (p. 8); ±1 SD error bars across apps in the cost plot [V] (p. 7). No significance tests for model differences; no run-to-run variance (single trial) [V] (pp. 6, 9).
58	
59	## 7. Key findings
60	1. Build success is 100% for all six models; authors attribute this to the harness's verify-repair loop, not the model [V] (pp. 6–7, 12).
61	2. NavPassRate: Opus 4.6 92%, GPT-5 89%, Haiku 4.5 85%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 82%, Gemini 2.5 Flash 62%, GPT-5 Mini 58% [V] (p. 7).
62	3. Visual fidelity has not saturated: Borda 0.906 (Opus) to 0.130 (GPT-5 Mini); point-wise means 1.60–2.99/5, so even the best model stays below 3/5; Opus leads in 26 of 29 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). The gap is concentrated in cross-page Consistency: models re-implement navigation chrome inline per page instead of sharing a component [A] (p. 6).
63	4. Maintainability is dissociated from visual fidelity: Opus writes 1,441 LoC (82 LoC/file) vs GPT-5 668 (33 LoC/file); GPT-5 has higher reuse (4.23 vs 3.83) and fewer dead components (7.8% vs 19.9%); ColorConsistency saturates at 0.74–0.85 [V] (pp. 6–7). Authors: "maintainability is uncorrelated with visual fidelity" [A] (p. 8) — no correlation coefficient is computed.
64	5. Cost: $0.15 (GPT-5 Mini) to $2.90 (Opus) per app; GPT-5 ($0.50, Borda 0.542, NavPass 89%) dominates Haiku 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on cost and quality [V] (p. 7). Cheaper models fabricate content (Lorem ipsum, stock imagery) [A] (p. 7).
65	6. Navigation failure taxonomy (n = 64 stratified hand-labelled failures from 3,486 executions): C1 blank starting page 7.8% [3.0, 18.3]; C2 route mapping error 10.9% [5.4, 20.9]; C3 target unreachable/occluded 32.8% [22.6, 45.0]; C4 click has no effect 48.4% [36.6, 60.4] [V] (p. 8). C4 (missing or mis-wired onClick) dominates for Opus and GPT-5 (75% of their labelled failures); C3 for GPT-5 Mini (67%); C1 for Gemini 2.5 Flash (42%) [V] (pp. 8, 15). Build checks do not catch silent event-handler bugs [A] (p. 8).
66	7. Per-app difficulty varies widely: point-wise visual 3.62 (Notion) to 2.01 (Apple News); NavPass 0.45 (Medium) to 1.00 (Khan Academy) [V] (pp. 7, 12).
67	
68	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
69	- Single trial per cell; multi-trial replication left to future work [A] (p. 9).
70	- Visual scores come from Gemini 2.5 Pro, a competitor model class; mitigated by fixed judge, human calibration on 55 scenarios and a cross-judge check [A] (p. 9).
71	- Web-rendering proxy: output is React + Tailwind, not native iOS/Android; native APIs not exercised [A] (p. 9).
72	- Anchor-based judging depends on judges that follow the literal ranking instruction (GPT-5.1 fails) [A] (pp. 13–14).
73	- Per-model failure proportions (n = 8–12) are "descriptive signatures rather than precise point estimates" [A] (p. 8).
74	- Build success cannot discriminate models when a verify-repair loop is present [A] (p. 12).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] Input is not screenshots alone: the agent also receives a human-reviewed page-relationship description (tab structure, parent–child triggers) (pp. 3, 6), although related work frames the benchmark as using "only screenshots" without "any structural prior" (p. 2). Results therefore describe reconstruction with an annotated navigation map, not pure black-box observation.
78	- [I] Maintainability indicators are structural proxies (LoC, reuse, dead components, colour tokens) with no validation against developer judgement or standard metrics (complexity, duplication, smells, tests). LoC partly reflects how much content is reproduced, so "more LoC" is not clearly worse (p. 4, 7).
79	- [I] "Uncorrelated"/"orthogonal" is asserted from six model means (p. 8); no correlation is computed at app or run level.
80	- [I] Internal inconsistency in failure analysis: overall C4 = 48.4% (Table 4, p. 8), but the per-scenario-type projection (Table 11, p. 16) gives C4 of only 33% (parent–child) and 3% (tab navigation), which cannot average to 48.4% over the 581 interactive specs. The projection method or labels may differ; this needs clarification.
81	- [I] Human validation of the visual judge: 55 scenarios with unreported number of raters, rater expertise and inter-rater agreement (p. 13); the protocol comparison uses only 3 scenarios × 5 models (p. 12).
82	- [I] Human reference labels were produced by the authors themselves ("We labelled 55 scenarios", p. 13), not by independent raters, so the judge validation is not independent of the benchmark designers (blinding to candidate identity is stated, p. 13).
83	- [I] NavPass counts a pass when the content hash "changes meaningfully" for overlays (p. 5) — a lenient criterion; Table 11 shows 1–10% false positives in flagged cases (p. 16), but overall evaluator precision/recall on passes is not reported.
84	- [I] Well-known apps chosen for "broad cultural recognition" (p. 3) are likely represented in model training data; contamination is not discussed.
85	- [I] Single run per cell with stochastic agents; differences of a few NavPass points (e.g. Opus 92% vs GPT-5 89%) may be within run-to-run noise.
86	- [I] Navigation evaluated only as page transitions; in-page behaviour, state, data and back-end logic are not tested.
87	
88	## 10. Threats to validity
89	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): annotations drafted by an unnamed VLM, possibly from the same families evaluated; Gemini 2.5 Pro is both judge and evaluated model, and the only self-preference check is a qualitative comparison against one other judge (Claude Sonnet 4.5) on 139 scenarios from 5 apps (p. 13); human reference labels for the judge were produced by the authors themselves (p. 13); popular apps may be memorised [I].
90	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 29 apps, 5–21 screens each; web proxy instead of native; one harness design; closed models only [I].
91	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): NavPass measures routing, not full functional fidelity; Borda is relative (ordinal) and depends on the set of models compared; maintainability proxies unvalidated [I].
92	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single trial; no significance tests between models; Wilson CIs only for the failure sample (n = 64), per-model n = 8–12 [I].
93	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): strong — benchmark, harness, evaluator and run artifacts released, one-command replay (pp. 9–10); decoding settings and drafting VLM not reported; closed models may change [I].
94	
95	## 11. Future research directions
96	- Stated by authors [A]: multi-trial replication (p. 9); cross-platform/native extension (p. 9); stricter build gates (no `any`, strict null checks, lint) if compilation is to discriminate models (p. 12).
97	- Suggested by us [I]: test pure screenshot-only input (without the page-relationship description) and interaction recordings as input; add in-page behavioural tests and data/state checks; validate maintainability proxies against developer ratings and standard static-analysis metrics; report run-to-run variance.
98	
99	## 12. Relevance to our research
100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
101	- How it informs our work [I]: MobileForge is the closest existing design to our target study: it rebuilds whole multi-screen apps from screenshots of real, in-market apps with an agentic (vibe-coding-like) harness and scores functional navigation fidelity, visual fidelity and maintainability together. It shows these dimensions diverge (visual leader ≠ maintainability leader), giving direct support for joint evaluation. Its gaps — structural prior given as input, unvalidated maintainability proxies, single trials, no behaviour beyond navigation — are concrete design points for RQ5.
102

105	|---|---|---|---|---|

18	# DeclarUI: Bridging Design and Development with Automated Declarative UI Code Generation
19	
20	- Authors: Zhou, Ting; Zhao, Yanjie; Hou, Xinyi; Sun, Xiaoyu; Chen, Kai; Wang, Haoyu
21	- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1145/3715726 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3715726
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index), extracted from arXiv:2409.11667v1 (18 Sep 2024), the pre-publication preprint, not the PACMSE (FSE 2025) published version; numbers, especially ablation Table 2, may differ in the published version (not checked)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- Propose DeclarUI, an automated approach that combines computer vision (CV), MLLMs and compiler-driven iterative refinement to generate multi-page declarative mobile UI code (React Native, Flutter, ArkUI) from UI design mockups or app screenshots, improving visual fidelity, navigation completeness and code quality [A] (pp. 1–2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- RQ1 Effectiveness: how does DeclarUI perform vs. baselines "when operating autonomously without human intervention"? [V] (p. 6)
33	- RQ2 Ablation: contribution of individual modules [V] (p. 6)
34	- RQ3 User study and manual repair: how do professional developers rate DeclarUI code vs. the baseline, and how much manual effort repairs compilation failures? [V] (p. 6)
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: technique proposal evaluated by a controlled comparison with two raw-MLLM baselines on a curated dataset, an ablation on a subset, a within-subject developer study, and a manual-repair timing study [V] (pp. 6–11).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: (1) Page Transition Graph (PTG) construction — Claude-3.5 infers nodes (pages) and edges (transitions with conditions/actions) from the design set as JSON; "designers or developers review the generated PTG, making necessary corrections or additions" [V] (pp. 3–4); (2) UI component extraction — Grounding DINO detection + Segment Anything segmentation + Claude-3.5 classification and functional description of each component [V] (p. 4); (3) prompt synthesis combining PTG, component analysis and the full screenshot [V] (p. 5); (4) iterative refinement — static-analysis check of implemented navigation vs. PTG (up to 3 iterations per page) and compile-error feedback (up to 3 iterations per project) [V] (pp. 5–6).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20240620 given unprocessed design images with "meticulously designed" prompts following prior image-to-code work, in React Native only [V] (p. 7). DeclarUI is run with GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 as base models; Flutter and ArkUI are run with DeclarUI (Claude-3.5) only, with no baseline [V] (pp. 8–9). No prior UI-to-code tool is used as a baseline [I] (based on p. 7).
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): Figma community mockups (selected from 194 designs with >300 followers, ≥5 pages, mobile-specific) and Google Play apps (top 10 by downloads per category, excluding paid apps and complex registration; APKs installed on an emulator and screenshots captured manually) [V] (pp. 6–7).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit: 50 apps (25 Figma, 25 Google Play), 5 logically connected pages each = 250 pages, 10 functional categories × 5 apps [V] (pp. 6–7). Ablation: 13 apps chosen by CLIP-score distribution across categories [V] (p. 9). User study: 12 apps stratified by CLIP score (3 > 0.85, 6 in 0.8–0.85, 3 < 0.8) [V] (p. 9). RAG experiment: 20 apps (100 pages) [V] (p. 11).
44	- Sampling / selection method: 3–5 per category per source, random selection of five when more available, "to control experimental costs while ensuring research quality and statistical significance" [A] (p. 7). Sample size limited "due to MLLMs' token cost constraints" [A] (p. 12).
45	- Data availability (public? link?): not reported in our PDF (no repository link found).
46	
47	## 5. Experimental setup
48	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: generated code inserted into an initial project in Android Studio (React Native, Flutter) or DevEco Studio (ArkUI) without manual intervention, built into an APK and run on the built-in emulator [V] (p. 8). Hardware: 2× RTX 3090, 64-core AMD EPYC, 512 GB RAM; custom Python scripts of 2,935 lines [V] (p. 8). UTG for evaluation obtained with DroidBot [V] (p. 7). Temperature, sampling settings and GPT-4o version: not reported. Image assets are excluded from evaluation [V] (p. 2).
49	- Code availability: not reported in our PDF.
50	
51	## 6. Evaluation metrics
52	- CLIP score — semantic visual similarity of generated vs original UI [V] (p. 7).
53	- SSIM — layout/structural similarity [V] (p. 7).
54	- PTG Coverage Rate PCR = |PTG edges ∩ UTG edges| / |PTG edges| × 100%, "manually calculated by human evaluators", comparing the predefined PTG with the DroidBot-explored UI Transition Graph of the built app — a navigation/functional-fidelity measure [V] (p. 7).
55	- Compilation Success Rate (CSR) — share of apps compiling after up to three automated refinement iterations [V] (p. 7).
56	- Average Compilation Iteration Count (ACIC) — compilation attempts per successfully compiled app (max 3) [V] (p. 7).
57	- Average Manual Correction Time (AMCT) — human repair time per compilation-failed app [V] (p. 7).
58	- Developer-rated code quality (user study, following Chen et al. [11]): Code Availability (proportion of generated code kept after modification to meet basic business requirements, tracked with git, mapped from 0.8 in 5% intervals to levels 1–5); Modification Time (5 points ≤5 min down to 1 point >20 min; 20-min cap per app); Readability and Maintainability (five-point Likert ratings) [V] (pp. 7, 9).
59	- Validation against human judgement: none for CLIP/SSIM; authors acknowledge they "may not fully capture human-perceived UI similarity" and state the user study "confirmed the validity of our evaluations" [A] (p. 12). No correlation between automatic metrics and human ratings is reported.
60	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Mann-Whitney U test for user-study ratings (p from 9.23E-08 to 2.57E-13) [V] (p. 10). No tests, CIs or run-to-run variance for CLIP/SSIM/PCR/CSR comparisons; no effect sizes — not reported.
61	
62	## 7. Key findings
63	1. React Native: DeclarUI (Claude-3.5) CLIP 0.88, SSIM 0.68, PCR 96.8%, CSR 98%; DeclarUI (GPT-4o) 0.87 / 0.58 / 88.6% / 88%; baselines GPT-4o 0.66 / 0.44 / 1.4% / 76% and Claude-3.5 0.65 / 0.41 / 43.3% / 74% [V] (p. 9).
64	2. Raw MLLMs largely fail to implement multi-page navigation (GPT-4o PCR 1.4%) [V] (p. 9). Baseline compilation failures came from non-existent packages/components, special-character handling and missing imports [A] (p. 8).
65	3. Generalisation: Flutter PCR 99.4%, CSR 92%; ArkUI PCR 95.9%, CSR 86% (DeclarUI Claude-3.5 only) [V] (p. 9). Knowledge-graph RAG for ArkUI on 20 apps: CSR 86% → 90%, AMCT 183 s → 43.5 s [V] (p. 11).
66	4. Ablation (13 apps): removing CV extraction drops SSIM 0.72 → 0.57; removing PTG + refinement drops PCR to 23.1% and CSR to 80% [V] (pp. 9–10).
67	5. User study (5 developers × 12 apps): DeclarUI vs Baseline (Claude-3.5) — availability 4.97 vs 4.15, modification time 4.03 vs 2.45, readability 4.62 vs 3.75, maintainability 4.55 vs 3.37, all p < 0.05 (Mann-Whitney U) [V] (p. 10). 73.3% of DeclarUI code modified within 10 min; 80% of baseline code needed >10 min [V] (p. 10).
68	6. Manual repair: AMCT 48 s (React Native, Claude-3.5), 43.2 s (GPT-4o), 62 s (Flutter), 183 s (ArkUI) [V] (p. 11).
69	7. Authors conclude generated code "meets industrial-grade standards" in availability, modification time, readability and maintainability [A] (pp. 1–2) — this rests on Likert ratings from five developers.
70	
71	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
72	- CLIP and SSIM may not capture human-perceived UI similarity; PCR does not reflect navigation fluidity or intuitiveness [A] (p. 12).
73	- Results depend on prompt design; user-study participant experience may bias results [A] (p. 12).
74	- Sample of 50 design sets may not represent all mobile UI types; limited by token cost [A] (p. 12).
75	- Uneven framework performance; ArkUI weaker, attributed to limited MLLM knowledge; RAG implementation limited by time [A] (p. 11).
76	- PTG construction could not be ablated alone because refinement depends on it [A] (p. 9).
77	
78	## 9. Limitations we identified
79	- [I] Human in the loop vs "autonomous" claim: the PTG is reviewed and corrected by designers/developers (p. 4), while RQ1 is framed as operating "without human intervention" (p. 6). How often and how much the PTG was corrected is not reported.
80	- [I] PCR is partly circular: DeclarUI receives the PTG as input and is checked against it during refinement, then scored against the same PTG (pp. 5–7); baselines never see the PTG. PCR also counts only edges, not correct behaviour on each screen, and is computed manually without reported agreement (p. 7).
81	- [I] Ablation numbers are internally implausible: on 13 apps, CSR values of 98.0% and 80.0% (p. 10) cannot arise (possible values are k/13, e.g. 76.9%, 84.6%, 92.3%). In the ablation table the "Full" row's CLIP/SSIM (0.90/0.72, p. 10) differ from the 50-app values (0.88/0.68, p. 9), while PCR/ACIC/CSR are identical to the 50-app run (96.8 / 0.22 / 98.0, pp. 9–10). This strongly suggests the visual metrics were recomputed on the 13 apps but PCR/ACIC/CSR were copied from the 50-app run (based on pp. 9–10); the ablation's PCR/CSR deltas are therefore not like-for-like comparisons.
82	- [I] User-study statistics treat 60 ratings per condition (5 developers × 12 apps) as independent; the tiny p-values (down to 2.57E-13, p. 10) overstate certainty (pseudo-replication). Blinding of participants to condition is not reported. Five participants is a small sample.
83	- [I] Code quality and maintainability are measured only subjectively (Likert) and by modification time; no static analysis, complexity, duplication or code-smell metrics.
84	- [I] Minor inconsistencies: Baseline Claude PCR 43.4% (p. 8) vs 43.3% (p. 9); ACIC defined as "number of compilation attempts" (max 3) yet reported as 0.22 (pp. 7, 9), implying it counts only repair iterations.
85	- [I] Single run per configuration; no variance across runs, though MLLM outputs are stochastic (sampling settings not reported).
86	- [I] Our PDF is arXiv v1 (18 Sep 2024); the FSE 2025 version may report different numbers.
87	
88	## 10. Threats to validity
89	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): human PTG correction; PCR scored against the method's own input; ablation subset chosen by CLIP score; possible training-data exposure of popular Google Play apps' UIs not discussed [I].
90	- External (generalisability of sample/context): 50 apps × 5 pages; only UI and navigation (no back-end, data, business logic); image assets ignored (p. 2) [I].
91	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): CLIP/SSIM unvalidated proxies for visual fidelity (p. 12); PCR measures presence of transitions, not their correctness of state; compilation success is a weak proxy for functional correctness; maintainability is self-reported [I].
92	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): Mann-Whitney on non-independent ratings; four tests without correction (not critical given p values); no CIs or effect sizes [I].
93	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): no code or data link in our PDF; model sampling settings missing; tools (Grounding DINO, SAM, DroidBot) named (pp. 4, 7) [I].
94	
95	## 11. Future research directions
96	- Stated by authors [A]: richer knowledge-graph RAG for less common frameworks such as ArkUI, dynamic KG updates, extension to other frameworks (p. 11); larger and more diverse UI samples (p. 12).
97	- Suggested by us [I]: report PTG correction effort; measure navigation and in-screen behaviour with automated GUI tests rather than manual edge counts; add objective maintainability metrics (static analysis, code smells) alongside developer ratings; use mixed-effects models for user-study ratings.
98	
99	## 12. Relevance to our research
100	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
101	- How it informs our work [I]: DeclarUI is one of few studies that rebuilds multi-screen mobile apps from screenshots of existing Google Play apps — a direct form of reverse engineering from observable UI — and it measures navigation fidelity (PCR via DroidBot exploration), compilability and developer-rated readability/maintainability together. It shows that structuring the observable behaviour (page transition graph) and compiler feedback matter, but its maintainability evidence is subjective and its fidelity metrics have design weaknesses.
102	
103	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
104	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
105	|---|---|---|---|---|
106	| RQ1 | Pipeline: Grounding DINO + SAM component extraction, MLLM-built page transition graph, compiler/navigation feedback loop for declarative mobile UI code | p. 3–6 | V | moderate |
107	| RQ1 | PTG is reviewed and corrected by designers/developers (human in the loop) | p. 4 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ2 | Navigation fidelity via PTG Coverage Rate (manual comparison with DroidBot UTG): DeclarUI 96.8% vs Claude-3.5 43.3% vs GPT-4o 1.4% (React Native, 50 apps) | p. 7, 9 | V | moderate |
109	| RQ2 | Compilation success 98% (DeclarUI Claude-3.5) vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs; CLIP 0.88 vs 0.65–0.66; SSIM 0.68 vs 0.41–0.44 | p. 9 | V | moderate |
110	| RQ2 | Without PTG + refinement, PCR falls to 23.1% | p. 10 | V | weak |
111	| RQ3 | Developer ratings (5 devs × 12 apps): readability 4.62 vs 3.75, maintainability 4.55 vs 3.37, Mann-Whitney p < 1e-11 | p. 10 | V | weak |
112	| RQ3 | Code quality/maintainability measured only by Likert ratings, code availability and modification time; no static metrics | p. 7, 9 | V | moderate |
113	| RQ4 | CLIP/SSIM acknowledged not to capture human-perceived similarity; no correlation with human ratings reported | p. 12 | A | moderate |
114	| RQ4 | Ablation CSR values (98%, 80%) impossible for 13 apps; user-study test ignores rating dependence | p. 9–10 | I | moderate |
115	| RQ5 | No back-end/business logic, image assets ignored; sample 50 apps limited by token cost | p. 2, 12 | A | moderate |
116	
117	## 14. Key quotes
118	> "Finally, designers or developers review the generated PTG, making necessary corrections or additions" (p. 4)
119	> "This metric, manually calculated by human evaluators, assesses the alignment between the implemented app structure and the intended design." (p. 7)
120	> "CLIP Score and SSIM, used for UI similarity assessment, may not fully capture human-perceived UI similarity" (p. 12)
121	
122	## Analyst notes
123	- Reading coverage: whole PDF read (pp. 1–13); reference list skimmed. Figure 7 heatmaps not inspected in detail (garbled in text; only summary statements used).
124	- Uncertainties: our PDF is arXiv v1 (Sep 2024), not the PACMSE/FSE 2025 published version; numbers may have changed. Ablation Table 2 numbers look inconsistent with a 13-app subset. Peer-reviewed (Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering, tier 1), but our copy is the preprint.

220	## Contradictions
221	<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->
222	
223	Each entry records both sides with page refs, then compares data, population, method, metric and time. Explanations are labelled [I]. We do not pick a side.
224	
225	### C1. Does AI assistance harm maintainability? he2026speed vs borg2026echoes
226	- **Side A** [V]: Cursor adoption in 806 OSS repositories raised total SonarQube static-analysis warnings by +30.26% and total cognitive complexity by +41.64% relative to matched controls (Borusyak DiD) [@he2026speed, p. 7]. The complexity effect stays significant after controlling for codebase size in the GMM (0.086, p<0.01) [@he2026speed, p. 8].
227	- **Side B** [V]: When a second developer evolved AI-co-developed code without AI, there was no significant difference in completion time [@borg2026echoes, p. 33], CodeHealth (8.49 vs 8.44) [@borg2026echoes, p. 38] or test coverage [@borg2026echoes, p. 35]. The only "significant" maintainability effect, a Bayesian +0.10 CodeHealth for code from habitual AI users, favours AI [@borg2026echoes, p. 39].
228	- **Differences**:
229	  - Data and population: real-world OSS repositories with ≥10 stars [@he2026speed, p. 4] vs one 2 KLoC Java/Spring Boot task done by 151 volunteer professionals [@borg2026echoes, p. 19; @borg2026echoes, p. 64].
230	  - Tool generation: an agentic IDE (Cursor Composer/agent) [@he2026speed, p. 2] vs late-2024 assistants (Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) [@borg2026echoes, p. 3; @borg2026echoes, p. 60].
231	  - Metric: repository-total warnings and cognitive complexity, which scale with code size [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a LoC-weighted file-level CodeHealth average plus a second developer's evolution time [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
232	  - Time: monthly panel of up to about 20 months [@he2026speed, p. 5] vs a single hand-off task.
233	  - Robustness: he2026speed's quality effects turn negative and non-significant under the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%) [@he2026speed, p. 16]. borg2026echoes is underpowered (75 of 128 planned participants; 80% power only for d≈0.66) [@borg2026echoes, p. 19].
234	- **Partial agreement** [V]: borg2026echoes' observational Phase 1 also found more duplication (23% vs 11%), more complex conditionals and very large code-volume outliers in AI-assisted code [@borg2026echoes, p. 30; @borg2026echoes, p. 46]. With size controlled, he2026speed finds no direct Cursor effect on warnings [@he2026speed, p. 8].
235	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two results need not conflict. Both fit "AI adds more code, and project-level totals rise with it, while per-file health and the short-term effort of the next developer are not clearly worse". The he2026speed effect depends on the estimator, and borg2026echoes can rule out only large effects. Neither study settles the question.
236	
237	### C2. Fewer or more static-analysis issues in LLM code? molison2025llm vs he2026speed
238	- **Side A** [V]: GPT-4o solutions had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged "bugs" than APPS human solutions (OR 0.00–0.019) [@molison2025llm, p. 8], and lower SonarQube fix effort on introductory and interview tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 7].
239	- **Side B** [V]: Cursor adoption raised repository SonarQube warnings by +30.26% [@he2026speed, p. 7].
240	- **Differences**:
241	  - Unit: per-solution odds of an issue in single-file stdin/stdout programs [@molison2025llm, p. 5] vs monthly repository totals [@he2026speed, p. 5].
242	  - Baseline: competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability [@molison2025llm, p. 9] vs matched non-adopting repositories, which may themselves use other AI tools [@he2026speed, p. 7].
243	  - Metric: the SonarQube "bug" category vs all reliability, maintainability and security warnings.
244	  - Leakage: molison2025llm's few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions [@molison2025llm, p. 4].
245	  - Time: GPT-4o in 2024 vs Cursor agents in 2024–2025.
246	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the results are not comparable. Both use SonarQube, but the units, baselines and code types differ, so neither one refutes the other. molison2025llm's smell results are themselves mixed: zero-shot code had 3.57x the odds of a smell on introductory tasks [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
247	
248	### C3. Which instrument measures the quality of AI code? zhu2026understanding vs SonarQube-based studies
249	- **Side A** [A]: zhu2026understanding chose PyExamine to separate structural and architectural smells from the "superficial linting issues" counted by SonarQube [@zhu2026understanding, p. 2; @zhu2026understanding, p. 4]. It found more Long Method smells in larger LLMs' code than in human code [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
250	- **Side B** [V]: SonarQube-based studies report fewer issues in LLM code [@molison2025llm, p. 8], a platform-dependent issue density (22.83 vs about 9 issues/KLOC) [@mota2026comparing, p. 5], or more warnings with adoption [@he2026speed, p. 7].
251	- **Context** [A]: technical-debt tools disagree on what counts as real debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 5], and SonarQube and general linters were not designed for LLM-specific debt [@ehsani2026faster, p. 22]. mota2026comparing calls SonarQube an auxiliary indicator only [@mota2026comparing, p. 6]. borg2026echoes argues that CodeHealth outperforms the SonarQube Maintainability Rating; note that its first author works for CodeScene, the vendor of CodeHealth [@borg2026echoes, p. 4; @borg2026echoes, p. 75].
252	- **Differences**: the tools differ (PyExamine, SonarQube, CodeHealth, MI), and so do the task types (algorithmic snippets, generated web apps, OSS repositories). zhu2026understanding's Exp I counts are small, unnormalised and untested [@zhu2026understanding, p. 7].
253	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the direction of "LLM vs human code quality" may depend on the measuring instrument. The field has no validated, size-normalised maintainability measure for AI-generated code.
254	
255	### C4. Does iterative feedback or self-repair help? pan2026functional vs tran2026vibe / zhou2025declarui / wu2026looks
256	- **Side A** [V]: On GPT-5.2, three one-shot strategies all lowered the aggregate non-functional score without raising functional correctness: self-repair, environment repair and planning (NF 46.1–49.9% vs 57.1% at baseline) [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
257	- **Side B**:
258	  - [V] Browser self-testing during generation correlates with accuracy across 16 models (r = 0.72) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7].
259	  - [V] Removing DeclarUI's page-transition graph plus refinement loop cuts navigation coverage to 23.1% [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10]. Its compile success is 98% vs 74–76% for raw MLLMs [@zhou2025declarui, p. 9].
260	  - [V]/[A] A tsc + vite verify-repair loop gives 100% build success for all six models [@wu2026looks, p. 6]. The authors attribute this to the loop [@wu2026looks, p. 12].
261	- **Further evidence** [A]: agents' own validation missed behavioural mismatches with the reference [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
262	- **Differences**:
263	  - Feedback type: generic one-shot repair of a whole Python repository [@pan2026functional, p. 8], targeted compile and navigation checks [@zhou2025declarui, p. 5], and build checks [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
264	  - Design: a single-model intervention (pan2026functional) vs an observational correlation across models, where the system prompt itself demands browser testing [@tran2026vibe, p. 16].
265	  - Outcome: non-functional quality (pan2026functional) vs compilation, navigation or build (zhou2025declarui, wu2026looks).
266	  - Circularity: zhou2025declarui scores navigation against the same graph that guides its refinement [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
267	- **Possible explanation** [I]: feedback improves the property it checks (compilation, build, navigation edges). Self-testing goes along with stronger models. No study shows that generic repair improves both behavioural fidelity and code quality, and the only study that measures quality after repair finds harm (single model, single run).
268	
269	### C5. Do rebuilds "look right but behave wrong"? chen2025iwr / lu2025webgen / xiao2025benchmarking vs bai2026recreationworld / wu2026looks
270	- **Side A** [V]:
271	  - Interactive functionality is below visual fidelity for all 28 models (GPT-5 IFS 24.39 vs VFS 64.25) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
272	  - Design-validation tests are passed more often than functional tests (e.g. 44.3% vs 21.1%) [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
273	  - Interactive regions score lower than full pages for all six models [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
274	- **Side B** [V]:
275	  - In bai2026recreationworld the visual (VLM) channel is below the programmatic channel for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11], although static structure beats actions within the programmatic tests [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
276	  - In wu2026looks navigation passes 58–92% [@wu2026looks, p. 7], while visual fidelity stays at or below 2.99/5 [@wu2026looks, p. 6].
277	- **Differences**:
278	  - chen2025iwr's VFS is averaged only over reached checkpoints, so part of its IFS<VFS gap comes from how the metrics are built [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
279	  - Visual scores come from different instruments: OCR+DINO+MLLM rubric, VLM assertions, Borda ranks and CLIP.
280	  - Functional scores also differ: action replay, accessibility tests and navigation tests.
281	- **Possible explanation** [I]: bai2026recreationworld and chen2025iwr are only *directionally consistent* on one point: static structure is reproduced more easily than interaction logic. The broader claim "visual fidelity systematically exceeds functional fidelity" is not supported, because the visual and functional scales are not commensurable across or within papers.
282	
283	### C6. Multi-agent / agentic frameworks: MetaGPT fails in liu2026benchmarking but leads in mock2026vibe
284	- **Side A** [V]: MetaGPT nearly always fails on E2EDev (0–5.4% Req.Acc) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6]. Multi-agent frameworks "do not consistently improve" over a plain LLM (by our count, 9 of 24 cells higher [I]) [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
285	- **Side B** [V]: Agentic MetaGPT X runs had the highest test pass rate (mean 94.58%) [@mock2026vibe, p. 25; @mock2026vibe, p. 41]. zhu2026understanding generated complete multi-file apps with MetaGPT, but only after adding explicit modularity prompts [@zhu2026understanding, p. 5].
286	- **Differences**:
287	  - Task size: a two-function string task [@mock2026vibe, p. 12] vs 46 multi-requirement web apps.
288	  - Backbone: GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4 [@mock2026vibe, p. 17] vs older or smaller backbones such as GPT-4o and Qwen2.5 [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 5].
289	  - Product: MetaGPT X web interface vs the open-source framework.
290	  - Evaluation: 12 runs pooled vs 46 projects x 3 runs.
291	- **Possible explanation** [I]: framework value depends on the backbone and the task scale. mock2026vibe's agentic advantage is confounded with the newer model generation.
292	
293	### C7. Security of generated code: pan2026functional vs zhao2025vibe
294	- **Side A** [V]: Reference-normalised security averages 87.40% and is the strongest non-functional dimension [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
295	- **Side B** [V]: 79.3% of the functionally correct solutions of the best agent fail targeted security tests, and SecPass is only 3.8–12.9% [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
296	- **Differences**: pan2026functional counts high-risk static findings relative to the reference, and the score can reward incomplete code. zhao2025vibe runs 3.5 targeted security tests per task for a known historical CWE [@zhao2025vibe, p. 5]. The tasks also differ: whole-repository generation vs security-sensitive feature patches.
297	- **Possible explanation** [I]: the two instruments measure different things, a static absence of flagged patterns vs exploit-relevant behaviour. "Secure" cannot be compared across them.
298	
299	### C8. More code or less code? Rebuilds are smaller, but assisted development adds code
300	- **Side A** [V]: Reconstructions are much smaller than their references. In bai2026recreationworld they are 89.4% smaller with 92.3% fewer files (4 of 10 models; desktop and Android only) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15]. In yang2026programbench they are shorter (median 1,173 vs 3,068 lines) and use fewer files [@yang2026programbench, p. 9].
301	- **Side B** [V]:
302	  - Cursor adoption raises lines added by +281.3% in month 1 [@he2026speed, p. 8].
303	  - AI-assisted Task 1 code produced outliers of up to 10,788 lines [@borg2026echoes, p. 30].
304	  - In MetaGPT apps, architectural smell counts track code size (ρ = 0.94) [@zhu2026understanding, p. 8].
305	  - The visual-fidelity leader writes 1,441 LoC vs 668 for GPT-5 [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
306	- **Differences**: rebuilds from scratch scored against a behavioural oracle of a mature original, vs incremental additions to existing projects or apps generated from a spec.
307	- **Possible explanation** [I]: reconstructions under-implement the original, which is consistent with low full-pass rates. Assisted development adds volume. Size therefore carries opposite signals in the two settings, and size-driven quality metrics (smell counts, totals) must be normalised before comparison.
308	
309	### C9. Apparent disagreements that come from different constructs (do not pool)
310	- **"Vibe coding" means different things** [V]:
311	  - fawzy2026vibe: natural-language prompting plus re-prompting with minimal review [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 1].
312	  - asdaque2026novice: a supervised agent workflow, operationalised as opening agentic PRs [@asdaque2026novice, p. 1]. Its authors warn that the findings may not hold under a broader definition [@asdaque2026novice, p. 4].
313	  - mock2026vibe: human-written TDD tests plus scripted prompts that participants could not modify [@mock2026vibe, p. 15].
314	  - he2026speed: Cursor configuration files committed to a repository (intent-to-treat) [@he2026speed, p. 4].
315	  - ehsani2026faster: a driver of fast-integration debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 17].
316	  - [I] These are different interventions. Their results should not be pooled as "effects of vibe coding".
317	- **Fidelity scores are not comparable** [V]:
318	  - 58.06% average of programmatic and VLM channels [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
319	  - 36.35 Final Score (0.7 IFS + 0.3 VFS) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8].
320	  - 49.15% cumulative workflows [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11].
321	  - 53.75% Req.Acc with `data-testid` anchors [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6].
322	  - 27.8% UI-agent accuracy with half credit for PARTIAL [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
323	  - 61.77% workflows passing at ≥90% of substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 6].
324	  - 0% resolved / 3% almost [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
325	  - [I] Each figure uses a different oracle, input, application type and model generation. Do not rank across them.
326	
327	### C10. Same model family builds or judges the benchmark and is evaluated (possible bias; untested)
328	- **Overlap and the same family wins** [V]:
329	  - yang2026programbench: Claude Sonnet 4.5 wrote the tests [@yang2026programbench, p. 3], and Claude models top the leaderboard [@yang2026programbench, p. 31].
330	  - tran2026vibe: GPT-5 drafted the specs [@tran2026vibe, p. 3], and GPT-5.3-Codex ranks first [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]. The canonical judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5 [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
331	  - kim2026programdistill: GPT-5.6 Sol builds the tasks [@kim2026programdistill, p. 2], GPT-6 Astra ranks first [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8], and GPT-6 Astra also classifies the failures [@kim2026programdistill, p. 12].
332	  - zhao2025vibe: Claude 4 Sonnet runs the environment-building agent [@zhao2025vibe, p. 17], and SWE-agent constructs the tasks [@zhao2025vibe, p. 4]. The best setting is SWE-agent + Claude 4 Sonnet [@zhao2025vibe, p. 7].
333	- **Overlap without a visible advantage** [V]:
334	  - liu2026benchmarking: GPT-4o built the annotations and is evaluated [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 13]; the best backbone is Claude-Haiku.
335	  - lu2025webgen: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and scored low [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
336	  - bai2026recreationworld: the Qwen3.7-Plus judge is the lowest-scoring model (average 9.15) [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11].
337	  - chen2025iwr: the Gemini-2.5-Pro judge ranks mid-table [@chen2025iwr, p. 7].
338	  - wu2026looks: the judge is Gemini 2.5 Pro, Opus leads [@wu2026looks, p. 13], and the authors report no self-preference [A].
339	- [I] No paper tests construction-model or judge-model self-preference directly. The pattern is a validity threat, not a demonstrated bias.
340	
341	## Agreements / converging evidence
342	
343	- **G-A1. Whole-application functional fidelity is far from complete** [V]. Every benchmark agrees:
344	  - Full behavioural equivalence: 2.8% of apps [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11] and 0 of 200 programs [@yang2026programbench, p. 6].
345	  - Best workflow-level or requirement-level pass rates: 49–62% [@kim2026programdistill, p. 11; @liu2026benchmarking, p. 6; @tran2026vibe, p. 6].
346	  - Lower still in some benchmarks: IFS <25 [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], <45% [@pan2026functional, p. 5], 27.8% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
347	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The direction is consistent across 8 independent benchmarks, but 5 of them are preprints and most use single runs.
348	- **G-A2. Behaviour and interaction are harder than static structure** [V]:
349	  - Structure beats actions [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 16].
350	  - Static tasks score higher than interactive ones [@chen2025iwr, p. 16].
351	  - Interactive parts score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
352	  - UI plus logic is harder than logic alone [@kim2026programdistill, p. 38].
353	  - "Click has no effect" is the largest navigation failure category (48.4%) [@wu2026looks, p. 8].
354	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**, with the measurement caveat in C5.
355	- **G-A3. Fidelity falls as dependency depth, size or complexity rise** [V]: [@kim2026programdistill, p. 8; @yang2026programbench, p. 31; @tran2026vibe, p. 6; @zhao2025vibe, p. 14]. Strength [I]: **moderate**.
356	- **G-A4. Functional correctness and other quality dimensions diverge** [V]:
357	  - Best static quality but lowest Pass@1 [@molison2025llm, p. 8].
358	  - Correct but insecure [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6].
359	  - Equal functional scores but very different non-functional scores [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
360	  - The visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
361	  - Authors state that passing functional tests does not imply maintainable code [A] [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
362	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**. The pattern is consistent, but each study measures a different second dimension.
363	- **G-A5. Rebuilt code is structurally simpler and more monolithic than the original** [V]: [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on 2 preprints, selected subsets and size proxies only.
364	- **G-A6. Code quality and maintainability are rarely measured in fidelity benchmarks**:
365	  - Not measured at all [V]: [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3; @xiao2025benchmarking, p. 5; @kim2026programdistill, p. 14].
366	  - Explicitly left out [A]: [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
367	  - Measured only by proxies [V]: size and structure [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9], LoC/reuse proxies [@wu2026looks, p. 4], a single MI index [@pan2026functional, p. 3], Likert ratings [@zhou2025declarui, p. 7].
368	  - Strength [I]: **strong** as a description of the field (verified absences across 12+ papers).
369	- **G-A7. LLM judges must be validated per judge model** [V]:
370	  - Judge–human agreement ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the evaluator model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9].
371	  - 86–94% raw agreement on 3 settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
372	  - τ = 0.716 on 55 author-labelled scenarios [@wu2026looks, p. 13].
373	  - ρ = 0.65, tuned in-sample [@chen2025iwr, p. 17].
374	  - Low human inter-annotator κ (0.26–0.46) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
375	  - Strength [I]: **moderate**.
376	- **G-A8. Practitioners perceive vibe-coded output as fast but flawed** [V]: [@fawzy2026vibe, p. 8]. This converges with LLM-linked code and design debt in mostly grey sources [@ehsani2026faster, p. 16] and with higher review burden for novice agent users [@asdaque2026novice, p. 3]. Strength [I]: **weak**. It rests on perception and proxy evidence, not code measurement.
377

## WebGen-Bench: Evaluating LLMs on Generating Interactive and Functional Websites from Scratch

> **Takeaway:** When AI coding agents build whole websites from a plain-language request, even the best early-2025 setup passes only 27.8% of the test cases, and visual or design requirements are met far more often than functional ones. A site can look right while its features do not work.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Zimu Lu, Yunqiao Yang, Houxing Ren, Haotian Hou, Han Xiao, Ke Wang, et al. (10 authors in our metadata; the arXiv PDF author line differs slightly) |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed. We read the arXiv v2 version, which is marked "Under review"; the published version may differ in details |
| Identifier | DOI 10.52202/085713-2419 · arXiv 2505.03733 |
| Paper type | Benchmark plus comparative evaluation, with a fine-tuning experiment |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ4; RQ5 by what it leaves out (no code quality) |

### In plain words
The authors ask a simple question: can an AI agent build a complete, working website on its own if you only describe what you want in everyday words? To answer it they built a benchmark, which is a fixed set of tasks plus an automatic way of scoring them, so that different AI systems can be compared fairly [@lu2025webgen, p. 3]. The tasks are 101 website requests, such as small business or data-management sites, and each comes with a list of things a user should be able to do [@lu2025webgen, p. 5]. A second AI then clicks through each generated site like a tester and reports whether each feature works [@lu2025webgen, p. 6]. This matters for us because it was one of the first studies to score whole AI-built apps by their behaviour, not just by how the code looks.

### How they did it
1. They collected 20 categories of web applications from freelance job platforms. Forty computer-science PhD students brainstormed 10,152 project ideas, and GPT-4o turned them into instructions [@lu2025webgen, p. 5].
2. They picked 101 instructions as the test set [@lu2025webgen, p. 5].
3. For each instruction, GPT-4o drafted 5–10 test cases. A test case is one small action plus the expected result (for example "click Add, a new row appears"). Two PhD students checked and corrected them, giving 647 test cases [@lu2025webgen, p. 6].
4. Three agent frameworks built the sites: Bolt.diy, OpenHands and Aider. An agent framework is the software around a language model that lets it write files and run commands on its own [@lu2025webgen, p. 7].
5. A "UI agent" (WebVoyager, driven by the Qwen2.5-VL-32B model) opened each site, tried each test case in at most 15 interactions, and answered YES, PARTIAL or NO [@lu2025webgen, p. 6].
6. Accuracy is (YES + 0.5 × PARTIAL) divided by all test cases. A site that does not start counts as a failure [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
7. GPT-4o also gave each site an appearance grade from 1 to 5 [@lu2025webgen, p. 6].
8. To check the automatic tester, three humans tested three settings by hand and their labels were compared with the UI agent's [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
9. Finally they fine-tuned (further trained) open Qwen2.5-Coder models on 600 recorded agent runs to see whether training helps [@lu2025webgen, p. 7].

### Data and setup
- 101 test instructions: 28 content presentation, 49 user interaction, 24 data management [@lu2025webgen, p. 6].
- 647 test cases: 339 functional, 186 data display, 122 design validation [@lu2025webgen, p. 23]. That table prints "Total 667", which is a typo; the categories add up to 647.
- Models included Claude-3.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, o3-mini and Qwen2.5 models, mostly inside Bolt.diy [@lu2025webgen, p. 7].
- One run per setting. Temperature and time budgets are not reported [@lu2025webgen, p. 40].
- Testing all 647 cases by hand would take about 10.8 hours and $377.8 per setting, which is why they automated it [@lu2025webgen, p. 6].
- Data, code and models are released under an MIT licence (author claim; we did not check the link) [@lu2025webgen, p. 1].

### Key findings
- [V] The best general-model setting, Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-R1, reaches only 27.8% accuracy; Bolt.diy with Claude-3.5-Sonnet reaches 26.4% [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
- [V] The framework matters a lot. With the same model (DeepSeek-V3), accuracy is 20.8% in Bolt.diy, 14.1% in Aider and 9.0% in OpenHands [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
- [V] Many sites never start: start failures reach 38.6% for Bolt.diy with o3-mini [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
- [V] Functional tests are much harder than design tests: 21.1% vs 44.3% for Bolt.diy with DeepSeek-R1, and 17.1% vs 52.0% with Claude-3.5-Sonnet [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
- [A] The authors conclude that "superficial aspects, such as color themes, are easier to implement than deeper internal functionalities" [@lu2025webgen, p. 8].
- [V] The UI agent agrees with the human label on 86.1–94.4% of test cases in the three checked settings [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
- [V] Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-32B on 600 runs lifts accuracy from 9.5% to 38.2%, and more training data helps (25.1% with 150, 31.9% with 300, 38.2% with 600) [@lu2025webgen, p. 10].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Only TypeScript, JavaScript, CSS and HTML sites; only supervised fine-tuning was tried [@lu2025webgen, p. 14].
- [A] No error bars "because it would be too computationally expensive" [@lu2025webgen, p. 40].
- [I] The human check covers only 3 of 16 settings, all in Bolt.diy. Agreement is raw percent with no chance correction, and agreement between the humans themselves is not reported [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
- [I] Most labels are NO (58–74%), so a tester that often says NO gets high agreement almost by default [@lu2025webgen, p. 9].
- [I] Each test checks one small visible feature, and PARTIAL earns half credit [@lu2025webgen, p. 8]. Deeper behaviour such as saved data or multi-step workflows is not tested.
- [I] With a single run, differences of 1–2 points (27.8 vs 26.4) cannot be told apart from noise.
- [I] The fine-tuning data was filtered by appearance score, not by functional tests [@lu2025webgen, p. 7].
- [I] No code quality, security or maintainability is measured.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors want more languages and tools, and other training methods (RL, DPO) [@lu2025webgen, p. 14].
- [I] G1: the generated code is never checked for quality or maintainability.
- [I] G2: GPT-4o wrote the test cases and is also evaluated. It scored low, so no advantage is visible [@lu2025webgen, p. 8], but bias was not tested. The released outputs could be re-judged in a G2 study [@lu2025webgen, p. 1].
- [I] G6: there is no human-developer baseline [@lu2025webgen, p. 7].
- [I] For reconstruction, tests would need to come from an existing site's observed behaviour, not from an instruction.

### Why it matters for your research
[I] WebGen-Bench set the pattern that many later benchmarks copy: AI-drafted, human-checked test cases run by a visual browser agent, plus a check against human testers. You can reuse this idea to score a rebuilt app against its original. Its main lesson for you is the gap between design and function: a rebuild that looks like the original may still fail on behaviour. Avoid two of its weak points in your own study: single runs, and judge checks on only a few settings without chance-corrected agreement.

### Connections to other papers
- Agrees with chen2025iwr, where interactive functionality scores below visual fidelity for all models (GPT-5: 24.39 vs 64.25) [@chen2025iwr, p. 8], and with xiao2025benchmarking, where interactive regions score lower than full pages [@xiao2025benchmarking, p. 6].
- Partly disagrees with bai2026recreationworld, where the visual channel scores below the programmatic channel for 9 of 10 models [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 11]. [I] The visual and functional scales differ across papers, so "looks right, works wrong" is only directionally supported.
- tran2026vibe builds on the same idea with multi-step browser workflows [@tran2026vibe, p. 4] and shows that judge agreement with humans ranges from 36.1% to 86.4% depending on the judge model [@tran2026vibe, p. 9]. [I] So the 86–94% here holds only for this judge.
- [I] Do not compare its 27.8% with E2EDev's 53.75% [@liu2026benchmarking, p. 6] or Vibe Code Bench's 61.77% [@tran2026vibe, p. 6]; each uses a different test method and scoring rule.

## Vibe Code Bench: Evaluating AI Models on End-to-End Web Application Development

|---|---|
| Authors | Hung Tran, Langston Nashold, Rayan Krishnan, Antoine Bigeard, Alex Gu |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · Proceedings of the ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems |
| Status | Peer-reviewed. We read the arXiv v3 version (May 2026); the ACM version was not compared |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813180 · arXiv 2603.04601 |
| Paper type | Benchmark plus comparative evaluation of 16 models, with a judge-reliability and variance study |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5; RQ3 as negative evidence (quality not measured) |

### In plain words

They also ask how far that AI judge can be trusted, by comparing it with human testers [@tran2026vibe, p. 9]. This matters for us because it is the closest benchmark to an autonomous vibe-coding build, and its browser-based scoring could be reused to compare a rebuild with its original.

### How they did it
1. Write tasks: a GPT-5 pipeline drafted 100 app specifications and their test workflows. Two product-manager reviewers accepted, changed or rejected each test, and an AI audit looked for mismatches [@tran2026vibe, p. 3].
2. Split: 50 apps for validation and 50 for the test set used in the main results [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
3. Build: each model worked inside a modified OpenHands container. This "harness" is the fixed environment around the model: a terminal, a browser and ready-made services for database (Supabase), email (MailHog) and payments (Stripe). Each app had up to 5 hours [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
4. Fix the technology: the system prompt required React + Vite, Tailwind, Supabase and Docker Compose, so that apps could be tested in the same way [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
5. Test: a Browser Use agent with Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the judge followed pre-written workflows and marked each small substep pass or fail. 6. Keep tests independent: each workflow starts in a fresh browser session with new account data [@tran2026vibe, p. 5].
7. Check variance: 6 specs × 3 models × 5 separate builds, plus 5 re-judgings of the same apps [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].
8. Check the judge: 18 apps (1,401 substeps) were tested by two of three humans who were blind to the model, and by four judge models [@tran2026vibe, p. 8].

### Data and setup
- 100 specifications, 964 workflows and 10,131 substeps; the test split has 50 apps, 473 workflows and 5,136 substeps [@tran2026vibe, p. 4].
- 28 of the 100 apps need payments and/or email [@tran2026vibe, p. 3].
- 16 models from 9 providers; no human developer or commercial tool baseline [@tran2026vibe, p. 5].

- [I] G3: the released apps could also test whether maintainability tools agree with each other.

## Toward Functional and Non-Functional Evaluation of Application-Level Code Generation

> **Takeaway:** When 16 AI models rewrite 38 real Python projects from a short description, none passes more than 45% of the tests, and code quality measured against the original is middling. It is one of the very few studies that scores working behaviour and code quality on the same generated apps, using the original project as the yardstick.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Ruwei Pan, Yakun Zhang, Qingyuan Liang, Yueheng Zhu, Chao Liu, Lu Zhang, Hongyu Zhang |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed) |
| Identifier | DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2602.03462 · arXiv 2602.03462 |
| Paper type | Benchmark (RAL-Bench) plus controlled empirical comparison of 16 models |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ1 secondary) |

### In plain words
Most code benchmarks test single functions or small fixes. The authors ask whether AI models can write a whole working application, with many files and dependencies, and whether that code is also good on qualities beyond "it works" [@pan2026functional, p. 1]. These other qualities are called non-functional: how maintainable, secure, robust, fast and resource-hungry the code is. They take real open-source projects as references, describe each in a short text, ask the AI to write the project, and test the result against the original [@pan2026functional, p. 2]. For us this is close to a joint "fidelity plus quality" study, although the AI never sees or runs the original app.

### How they did it
1. Pick projects: 38 maintained Python projects on GitHub (for example click, requests, celery), each frozen at a fixed version, in seven scenario groups [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
2. Write requirements: a short natural-language description built from the project's README, API, examples and code, then edited to remove implementation details and project names [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
3. Add an interface specification: the list of modules and packages the result should expose [@pan2026functional, p. 4].
4. Generate: each model writes the whole repository in one go, "zero-shot" (no examples and no second attempt). Each model runs 3 times and scores are averaged [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
5. Test behaviour: black-box tests (tests that only check inputs and outputs, not the code inside) are kept only if they pass on the original. The functional score is the share of tests passed [@pan2026functional, p. 4].
6. Test quality: five dimensions, each compared with the original and capped at 1 [@pan2026functional, p. 3]. Maintainability uses the Maintainability Index (MI), a formula that turns code complexity and size into one number. Security counts high-risk findings from static analysis (automatic code scanning without running it). Robustness, efficiency and resource use (memory and CPU) come from extra test runs [@pan2026functional, p. 4].
7. Combine: the five dimensions are weighted (maintainability 0.36, security 0.24, robustness 0.16, efficiency 0.12, resource 0.12) into one non-functional score (NF) [@pan2026functional, p. 4].
8. Extra studies: a failure analysis, costs, three improvement strategies on GPT-5.2, prompt wording, and different weightings [@pan2026functional, p. 5].

### Data and setup
- 38 projects of 1 to 242 files and 0.3k to 109.5k lines of code [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
- About 11 functional tests per task on average (minimum 10, maximum 19) [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
- 16 models: 11 "standard" and 5 "thinking" (reasoning) models, 3 runs each [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
- 76 deliberately injected bugs (2 per task) to check that the tests catch errors [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
- The pipeline was rerun 5 times for three models to check stability [@pan2026functional, p. 7].
- Greedy decoding is stated only in the abstract [@pan2026functional, p. 1]. Scripts and data are released (author claim) [@pan2026functional, p. 11].

### Key findings
- [V] Functional correctness is low: on average 33.98% for standard and 30.23% for thinking models, and no model exceeds 45%. The best is Gemini-3-Pro-Preview at 43.86%; the lowest is DeepSeek-R1 at 16.23% [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
- [V] Non-functional scores average 52.25% (standard) and 49.57% (thinking). Security is the strongest dimension (87.40% / 85.32%). Resource usage is the weakest (31.25% / 28.92%), with maintainability close behind (33.45% / 31.38%) [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
- [V] Quality separates models that function equally well: Gemini-2.5-Pro and GPT-4o both score about 27.6% functionally, but 35.15% vs 57.59% on NF [@pan2026functional, p. 5].
- [V] Thinking models are not consistently better [@pan2026functional, p. 6].
- [V] 82.8% of failures happen after the code runs (wrong behaviour or poor quality); 17.2% are install or start-up failures [@pan2026functional, p. 7].
- [V] Cost per run ranges from $0.15 to $16.63, and paying more does not reliably buy correctness [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
- [V] On GPT-5.2, self-repair, environment repair and planning all failed to beat the baseline (41.80% functional, 57.10% NF) and all lowered NF, to 46.10–49.90% [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
- [V] Giving the module list raised one task's functional score from 0.1667 to 0.6667 [@pan2026functional, p. 4]. Rewording the prompt moved GPT-5.2 from 0.4181 to 0.4972 [@pan2026functional, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] The projects are public, so the authors "do not claim that pretraining exposure can be fully ruled out" [@pan2026functional, p. 2].
- [A] MI misses naming quality and architecture; static security scans give false alarms and misses; all metrics are proxies, not expert audits [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
- [A] One-shot generation does not represent iterative, agent-based work; the strategy study uses one model [@pan2026functional, p. 8].
- [I] About 11 tests is a thin check for projects of up to 109.5k lines, and 2 injected bugs per task is a weak test of the tests.
- [I] Memorisation looks likely: the example requirement names the original "Stegano project" [@pan2026functional, p. 3], and one output used internals of the real Celery library [@pan2026functional, p. 9].
- [I] The quality score can reward incomplete code. GPT-3.5-Turbo scores 97.37% on security but 29.76% on function [@pan2026functional, p. 6]; less code means fewer findings.
- [I] The maintainability score equals 0.5, not 1, when the rebuild matches the original [@pan2026functional, p. 3], yet it has the largest weight.
- [I] Zero variance across 5 reruns [@pan2026functional, p. 7] is surprising and may mean cached outputs were re-tested. The authors call the prompt effect small, but it is about 30–40% of the spread between models.
- [I] Python libraries only; no user interfaces are tested.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] The authors propose quality-aware generation, repair across modules, and multi-turn, agent-based evaluation [@pan2026functional, p. 10].
- [I] G1: this is the only reference-anchored maintainability score in our corpus, but it is a single MI proxy, from text requirements rather than observed behaviour [@pan2026functional, p. 3].
- [I] G4: does feedback improve function and quality together? Here it harmed quality, for one model and one-shot strategies.
- [I] G5 and G7: memorisation and interface hints may inflate scores; neither effect is measured.
- [I] G3: whether MI agrees with other quality tools is untested.

### Why it matters for your research
[I] This paper shows the design you want, in rough form: measure behaviour and quality on the same rebuild and use the original as the baseline. Reuse the idea of tests kept only if they pass on the original, and of quality scores relative to the original. Improve on it: use richer, size-normalised quality measures, more tests, an iterative workflow, and controls for memorisation. Its result that repair strategies lowered quality is a warning for vibe-coding loops, but it is weak evidence (preprint, one model).

### Connections to other papers
- [V] Disagrees on security with zhao2025vibe, where 79.3% of functionally correct solutions fail targeted security tests [@zhao2025vibe, p. 6]. [I] Static counts and attack-style tests measure different things.
- [V] Conflicts on feedback with tran2026vibe (browser self-testing correlates with accuracy, r = 0.72) [@tran2026vibe, p. 7] and zhou2025declarui (refinement loop lifts navigation) [@zhou2025declarui, p. 10]. [I] Those loops check the very thing they score; this one measures quality after repair.
- [V] Agrees that function and quality diverge: in wu2026looks the visual leader is not the maintainability leader [@wu2026looks, p. 7].
- [V] Rebuilds elsewhere are much smaller than their originals [@bai2026recreationworld, p. 15; @yang2026programbench, p. 9]. [I] That is why size-sensitive quality scores like this one need care.
- [V] borg2026echoes offers a stronger maintainability test: a second developer evolves the code [@borg2026echoes, p. 13].
